subject: classical-electromagnetism

items.title: Complex plane-wave fields: real parts of complex exponentials
items.statement: Fix $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, $\omega>0$ and $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$. Writing $\exp$ for the complex exponential, $\operatorname{Re}$ for the real part and $\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x$ for the Euclidean inner product, define for each $t\in\mathbb R$ the real vector fields $$\mathbf x\mapsto\operatorname{Re}\bigl[\mathbf e\exp(i(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t))\bigr],\qquad \mathbf x\mapsto\operatorname{Re}\bigl[\mathbf b\exp(i(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t))\bigr]$$ on $\mathbb R^3$, componentwise. Complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations; the complex object is not itself a physical field, and real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are explicit operations.
items.strategy: State the encoding convention and its regularity: the defining maps are smooth in $(\mathbf x,t)$ because the complex exponential is entire and $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t$ is linear. No electromagnetic interpretation is asserted; that is a later model choice.

references.title: Review of Phasor Notation (course notes, University of San Diego), Complex Vectors and Time Harmonic Representation; Amplitude, Time Average, Mean Square
J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1

items.title: Moving parametrized surface patches and their flux
items.statement: Let D be a nonempty compact finite elementary Green region with its supplied positive boundary chain, I an interval (empty and singleton allowed), and r:D x I -> R^3 the restriction of a C^2 extension. Require r_u cross r_v nonzero on D interior x I interior, and a given C^1 velocity v on an open subset of R^4 containing the spacetime graph with v(r(p,t),t)=r_t(p,t). For a C^1 field B on a spacetime neighbourhood of that graph define Phi(t)=integral_D <B(r(p,t),t),r_u cross r_v> du dv. Parametrized flux allows disconnected/noninjective slices. Injectivity alone does not imply slice regularity; a regular material-slice interpretation also imposes nonzero cross product on D interior x I, including endpoint and singleton times. Singleton time jets depend on the chosen extension, while the flux does not.
items.strategy: Elementary Green regions are compact Jordan-measurable parameter regions, so the flux is a Riemann integral, and the orientation is the patch orientation of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. Single-valuedness of the velocity is the hypothesis that makes the transport formula of the moving-flux lemma well posed. No physical assertion is made.

references.title: M. E. Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables, §3.2 and §4.4
J. Feldman, A. Rechnitzer, E. Yeager, CLP-4 Vector Calculus (UBC), §4.1 (Theorems 4.1.4-4.1.16)

items.title: Surface distributions and interfacial jumps
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$, and put $\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS$ for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, the surface integral being that of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. A continuous density $a$ on $S$ defines $a\delta_S(\psi)=\int_S a\psi\,dS$. Both functionals are continuous of finite order on test functions, because $\lvert a\rvert$ and $\psi$ are bounded on the compact interface and the surface measure is finite. A field that is $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided continuous traces has locally integrable components; write $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ for the jump across $S$.
items.strategy: Use the compact surface integral definition and the finite-order estimate for continuous densities; for non-compact interfaces localize with a compactly supported test. The jump $[F]$ is the one-sided trace difference, and the sign convention of $n$ (minus to plus) is fixed here and used by the interface-derivative lemma.

references.title: S. Dyatlov, Lecture notes for 18.155 (MIT, 2026), Chapter 2 and Chapter 3
J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7

items.title: Localization: vanishing integrals or fluxes force a continuous function to vanish
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]).

**Integral form.** Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be continuous. Write $g_i(x):=g(x)(i)$ for $0\le i<m$, using the canonical function coordinates of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For a measurable $V\subseteq U$ write, componentwise,

$$\int_V g\,d\lambda_n:=\Bigl(\int g_0\chi_V\,d\lambda_n,\ \dots,\ \int g_{m-1}\chi_V\,d\lambda_n\Bigr),$$

each component $0\le i<m$, when integrable, being the Lebesgue integral of $g_i$ on $V$, extended by zero outside $V$ ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). A ball $V\subseteq U$ is **compactly contained** in $U$ when its closure is a compact subset of $U$; for a Euclidean ball this means $\overline V\subseteq U$. If $\int_Vg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for every ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$, then $g=0$ on $U$.

**Disc form.** Let $W\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:W\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Write $F_i(x):=F(x)(i)$ for $0\le i<3$ and $e_0=(1,0,0)$, $e_1=(0,1,0)$, $e_2=(0,0,1)$, the canonical standard vectors of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]. Extend the basis labels cyclically by $e_j:=e_{j\bmod3}$ for $j\ge3$. Thus $e_{i+1}\times e_{i+2}=e_i$ for each $i\in\{0,1,2\}$. For such $i$, $q\in W$ and $r>0$ put

$$\varphi_{i,q}(s,t):=q+s\,e_{i+1}+t\,e_{i+2},\qquad D_r:=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb R^2:s^2+t^2<r^2\},$$

with $\overline{D_r}$ the closed disc. If for every $i$, every $q\in W$ and every $r>0$ with $\varphi_{i,q}(\overline{D_r})\subseteq W$ one has

$$\int_{\overline{D_r}}(F_i\circ\varphi_{i,q})\,d\lambda_2=0,$$

then $F=0$ on $W$.

**Conventions.** The displayed disc condition is the vanishing of the flux of $F$ through the flat disc $\varphi_{i,q}(\overline{D_r})$ in the orientation with unit normal $e_i$: the affine parametrization is a regular patch whose tangent vectors $e_{i+1},e_{i+2}$ have cross product $e_i$ of norm one ([[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), so the flux of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]] is the Riemann integral $\int_{\overline{D_r}}(F_i\circ\varphi_{i,q})\,d(s,t)$; that integral equals the displayed Lebesgue integral because the integrand is continuous on the compact Jordan region $\overline{D_r}$ ([[cor-disc-jordan-content-is-pi-r-squared]], [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], [[lem-bounded-borel-riemann-integrands-on-boxes-have-equal-lebesgue-integrals]]). Both clauses are pointwise conclusions on their open domains. The first clause is the converse from universal integral relations to a pointwise equation; a single vanishing integral over one ball or one disc supplies no conclusion, and the hypothesis ranges over the full family described.
items.strategy: If $g(p)_i>0$, continuity gives a ball $V\Subset U$ on which $g_i\ge g_i(p)/2$; then $0<(g_i(p)/2)\lambda(V)\le\int_Vg_i$, contradicting the hypothesis. Apply to each component and to $-g_i$. The disk statement applies the planar case to each coordinate component with the coordinate normal. One special loop or box does not suffice.

references.title: J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7
J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1

items.title: Monopole-dipole expansion with an explicit remainder for compactly supported $L^1$ densities
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\lambda_3)$ be a real or complex valued Lebesgue integrable function on $\mathbb R^3$ that vanishes $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $B_a:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2\le a\}$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-metric-ball]]). Put

$$Q:=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p:=\int y\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3\in\mathbb C^3,\qquad \lVert\rho\rVert_1:=\int\lvert\rho\rvert\,d\lambda_3,$$

the vector $p$ being defined by $p_k:=\int y_k\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$ for the canonical coordinates $k<3$, namely $k\in\{0,1,2\}$, and $\langle p,x\rangle:=\sum_{k<3}p_kx_k$ being the complex-bilinear coordinate contraction, with no complex conjugation, which agrees with the real Euclidean pairing when $p$ is real; if $\rho$ is real-valued then $Q$ is real and $p\in\mathbb R^3$, while $R(x)$ below is real in that case and complex in general. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ with $r:=\lVert x\rVert_2\ge2a>0$,

$$\int\frac{\rho(y)}{\lVert x-y\rVert_2}\,d\lambda_3(y)=\frac Qr+\frac{\langle p,x\rangle}{r^3}+R(x),\qquad R(x):=\int_{B_a}\rho(y)\Bigl(\frac1{\lVert x-y\rVert_2}-\frac1r-\frac{\langle x,y\rangle}{r^3}\Bigr)d\lambda_3(y),$$

and the remainder satisfies the explicit bound

$$\lvert R(x)\rvert\le\frac{16\,a^2\,\lVert\rho\rVert_1}{r^3}.$$

In the all-space kernel integral define $K_x(y)=\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{-1}$ for $y\ne x$ and $K_x(x)=0$, so its integrand means $\rho K_x$ and is an everywhere-defined measurable function. This convention cannot affect the integral: $x\notin B_a$ and the density vanishes almost everywhere outside $B_a$. All integrals are Lebesgue integrals; the closed ball $B_a$ is Borel and $\chi_{B_a}\rho$ is integrable. The constant $16$ is permissible but not sharp, and $Q$, $p$ and $\lVert\rho\rVert_1$ are finite. No derivative of the remainder in $x$ is asserted.
items.strategy: Set $h(s)=\lvert x-sy\rvert^{-1}$; $h$ is $C^2$ on $[0,1]$ and the identity $h(1)-h(0)-h'(0)=\int_0^1(1-s)h''(s)\,ds$ follows from the fundamental theorem applied to $\frac{d}{ds}[(1-s)h'(s)+h(s)]=(1-s)h''(s)$. Because $\lvert x-sy\rvert\ge r-a\ge r/2$ for $r\ge2a$, one has $\lvert h''(s)\rvert\le4\lvert y\rvert^2/(r-a)^3\le32\lvert y\rvert^2/r^3$, and integrating against $\lvert\rho\rvert$ gives the bound with $C=16$, which is permissible but not sharp. Both leading terms follow directly by integrating h(0)=1/r and hprime(0)=(x dot y)/r³; no normalization-sensitive decay theorem is needed as a logical supplier. The parameter integral in $s\in[0,1]$ is a continuous Riemann integral, so [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]] bounds it by $32|y|^2r^{-3}\int_0^1(1-s)ds=16|y|^2r^{-3}$. The subsequent integral against the $L^1$ source density is Lebesgue: its majorant $16a^2r^{-3}|\rho|$ is handled by [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], not by the Darboux theorem. Both $Q$ and $p$ are finite by the same bounded-support estimate. No derivative bound on an unspecified remainder is inferred. Choose an a.e.-equal representative zero off the closed source ball. The integral equality and all moments are unchanged by [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]; every bound is thus valid for the declared a.e. support hypothesis.

references.title: J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7
S. Teitel, PHY 415 (University of Rochester), Unit 2-4: Electric Multipole Expansion

items.title: Differentiation under the integral sign over a compact measurable set and over a compact $C^1$ surface
items.statement:
**Set form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]), used to establish the Lebesgue measure space of [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]. Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.
items.strategy: For fixed $x$ the mean value theorem writes $[f(x,t+h)-f(x,t)]/h=\partial_tf(x,\tau)$ for some $\tau$ between $t$ and $t+h$; uniform continuity of $\partial_tf$ on the compact product bounds the integral of the difference by the sup-error times the finite measure. Iterate on finitely many charts, using the independence of the surface integral from the chart, for the surface clause.

references.title: J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1
J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7

items.title: Distributional continuity of a moving point charge
items.statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ a $C^1$ trajectory, and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ open containing its graph. Assume the graph map $\gamma:I\to\Omega$, $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$, is proper: the inverse image of every compact subset of $\Omega$ is compact in $I$. For $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ define $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ and $\langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_I z'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$. These define distributions and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. Properness is automatic if $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, or if $I=\mathbb R$. Endpoint variant: if $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite, and both endpoint events belong to $\Omega$, the same integrals instead define distributions with $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\delta_{(z(b),b)}$. A finite-history source is source-free only when the endpoint contribution vanishes on the chosen test domain; neither mere graph containment nor test compactness alone supplies this.
items.strategy: For a fixed compact test support $K\subset\Omega$, properness makes $\gamma^{-1}(K)$ compact in $I$. It lies in one closed interior interval $[u,v]\subset I$, on which $z'$ is bounded. Both pairings are bounded by constants depending on $K$ times $\sup_K|\psi|$, proving distribution continuity on each test-support space. The pullback of a test is $C^1$ and compactly supported in $I$. By the total chain rule, pairing the divergence gives $-q\int_I[\partial_t\psi(z(t),t)+z'(t)\cdot\nabla\psi(z(t),t)]dt=-q\int_I(d/dt)\psi(z(t),t)dt=0$ by interior FTC. For $I=\mathbb R$, compact ambient support bounds the time coordinate and its graph preimage is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R$; for $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, compact ambient support has time projection compact inside $I$. This proves both automatic properness claims. In the endpoint variant, finite interval length and the finite absolute improper integral of $z'$ bound the pairings on every compact test support. Apply the chain rule and FTC on $[a+\epsilon,b-\epsilon]$; the derivative pullback is absolutely integrable, and continuity at endpoints gives the limiting identity $q\psi(z(a),a)-q\psi(z(b),b)$. This proves the two endpoint deltas. In particular $I=(0,1),z=0,\Omega=\mathbb R^4$ gives $q\delta_{(0,0)}-q\delta_{(0,1)}$, refuting the old unconditional claim. The endpoint integration limit is explicitly this truncation argument, not an invented source reading. Maxwell existence and point self-force are not asserted. Here the two-ended improper integral means the sum of the limits of integrals on [a+epsilon,r] and [r,b−epsilon] for any fixed interior r. Monotonicity and completeness prove convergence of every nonnegative integrand bounded by a constant times 1+|z′|; signed limits then follow from the positive and negative parts. Thus the endpoint variant uses only the explicitly supplied improper convention and truncated ordinary FTC.

references.title: S. Dyatlov, Lecture notes for 18.155 (MIT, 2026), Chapter 2 and Chapter 3
J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7

items.title: Quadratic stress identity and the local angular-balance identity
items.statement:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), with coordinates $x_1,x_2,x_3$, partial derivatives $\partial_j=\partial/\partial x_j$, Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and norm $\lvert\cdot\rvert_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), divergence and curl as in [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and cross product as in [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Put

$$Q_{ij}:=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert_2^2,\qquad \delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases}\qquad (\operatorname{div}Q)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_jQ_{ij}.$$

Then $Q$ is a $C^1$ tensor field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}Q=F\,\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F .$$

Moreover, writing $\epsilon_{ijk}$ for the Levi-Civita symbol ($\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ if it is an odd permutation, and $0$ if two indices coincide), every symmetric tensor $Q$ (that is, $Q_{kj}=Q_{jk}$ for all $j,k$) satisfies

$$\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}=0\qquad(i\in\{1,2,3\}),$$

the sum over $j,k$ being the nine-term sum with each pair counted separately. Finally, if $\Pi$ is a $C^1$ symmetric tensor field on $U$, if $g:U\to\mathbb R^3$ is continuous, and if $\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ holds at every point of $U$ for a continuous $f:U\to\mathbb R^3$, where $(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i=\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\partial_\ell\Pi_{i\ell}$ and $(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}:=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell}$ with the sum over $j,k$, then the vector field $x\times g$ and the tensor field $x\times\Pi$ satisfy

$$\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f .$$

No symmetry of $Q$ beyond the displayed form is assumed, and no boundary integral is asserted: these are pointwise identities on $U$.
items.strategy: Expand $\sum_j\partial_j(F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert^2)=F_i\operatorname{div}F+\sum_jF_j\partial_jF_i-\sum_jF_j\partial_iF_j$ by the product rule; the last difference is $-(F\times\operatorname{curl}F)_i$. For the second part, expand $\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\partial_\ell\Pi_{k\ell}$ and cancel the two equal terms using symmetry; the term $\epsilon_{ijk}\Pi_{kj}$ vanishes. No symmetry of $Q$ beyond the displayed form is needed.

references.title: J. Feldman, A. Rechnitzer, E. Yeager, CLP-4 Vector Calculus (UBC), §4.1 (Theorems 4.1.4-4.1.16)

items.title: Distributional divergence and curl across a stationary interface
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $S\subset\Omega$ be a two-sided compact embedded $C^2$ interface with unit normal $n$ from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, and let $F$ be $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided $C^1$ traces on $S$. Then, away from the edge $\partial S$ and in the distributional sense, $$\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S,\qquad \operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[F]\,\delta_S,$$ where the bracket terms denote the locally integrable functions equal to the classical divergence and curl on each open side and $[F]=F_+-F_-$.
items.strategy: Against a test supported away from the edge, split $-\int F\cdot\nabla\psi$ into the two sides and apply the divergence theorem to $\psi F$ on each side; the outward normal is $n$ on the minus side and $-n$ on the plus side, so the boundary terms combine to $(F_+-F_-)\cdot n$. Componentwise integration by parts gives $\partial_iF_j=\{\partial_iF_j\}+n_i[F_j]\delta_S$, and antisymmetrizing the index pair gives the curl formula. A moving interface needs a separate account.

references.title: J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7
S. Dyatlov, Lecture notes for 18.155 (MIT, 2026), Chapter 2 and Chapter 3

items.title: Joint regularity of radial vector and scalar potentials on star-shaped domains
items.statement:
**Regularity convention for a possibly non-open parameter interval.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $k\in\mathbb N$. A map on $U\times I$ is **jointly $C^k$** when it is the restriction of a $C^k$ map on some open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; it is **jointly $C^\infty$** when it is the restriction of one smooth map on such an open neighbourhood. For open $I$ these are exactly the usual open-domain classes; at included endpoints of a nondegenerate interval, time derivatives are the corresponding relative one-sided derivatives. For empty or singleton $I$ the convention still asserts extension existence and the spatial identities below, but it does not determine time jets uniquely from the restricted values alone. The convention does not require a fixed uniform enlargement of an unbounded $I$.

**Vector witness.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a\in U$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Then

$$A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr)\times(x-a)\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the curl being taken in the spatial variables and the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

**Scalar witness.** If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$, then

$$\phi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\bigl\langle C\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr),\,x-a\bigr\rangle\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the gradient and inner product being those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For jointly $C^\infty$ data both potentials are jointly $C^\infty$. No global potential on a non-star-shaped open set is claimed, and the restrictions are continuous at included endpoints by joint regularity.
items.strategy:
The interval regularity convention is supplied explicitly in the statement, rather than treating the imported open-domain definition as already covering non-open products. To prove regularity in that same extension sense, choose an open-neighbourhood Ck extension of the data (intersect the extensions' neighbourhoods if both B and C are used). Let P be the set of (x,t) for which every (a+s(x-a),t), 0<=s<=1, lies in that open extension domain. It contains UxI by star-shapedness. It is open: at any one point of P its compact radial segment has a finite cover by balls contained in the extension domain; equivalently its distance from the closed complement is positive, and continuity of the radial map uniformly in s keeps all nearby (x,t) segments inside those balls. The identical radial integral of the extension data is therefore defined on P and is Ck there by the compact parameter proof below; its restriction is the stated potential. For smooth input use its one smooth extension and the same argument through every finite order. Curl-freeness/divergence-freeness is only needed on the original slices to establish the field identities there, not on the enlarged neighbourhood. Set w=x-a and z_s=a+sw. The spatial star-shaped hypothesis puts z_s in U for 0<=s<=1. For any compact spatial box Q contained in U and compact parameter subinterval J contained in I, the radial image of [0,1]xQ is compact inside U. Each component of the vector and scalar radial integrands is a finite sum of products of the polynomial factors s,w and the Ck components of B(z_s,t) or C(z_s,t). Chain and product rules give every mixed spatial/time word derivative through total order k as a continuous function of (s,x,t) on the corresponding compact product. Apply thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle in each parameter coordinate, with others fixed, and induct on derivative order. Uniform continuity on the compact product and lem-uniform-integral-error-bound show that each resulting derivative integral is jointly continuous. Included endpoints of nondegenerate time intervals use the relative endpoint derivatives of the compact-rectangle supplier. For empty or singleton I, construct the potentials using a chosen ambient extension on its open radial-admissibility set and restrict; this proves the same extension existence and spatial identities, without claiming uniquely determined time jets on the degenerate restriction. Thus both explicit integrals are jointly Ck, without assuming k+1 derivatives, and applying this for every k gives the smooth assertion. No surface-measure or Lebesgue integration/Choice branch of lem-em-parameter-integrals is needed: these are ordinary one-dimensional integrals in s on [0,1].

At each fixed t, the positive vector integral is exactly the witness of thm-a-divergence-free-c1-field-on-a-star-shaped-open-set-has-a-vector-potential, so curl A=B. For the scalar branch put Psi_C(x,t)=integral_0^1 <C(z_s,t),w> ds, and take phi_C=-Psi_C. The published Poincare theorem gives grad Psi_C=C; its convention is positive gradient, so it cannot itself justify grad of the positive integral being -C. Explicitly, curl C=0 means partial_j C_i=partial_i C_j in three dimensions. Differentiation gives partial_j Psi_C=integral_0^1 [C_j(z_s,t)+s sum_i w_i partial_j C_i(z_s,t)] ds. Replace partial_j C_i by partial_i C_j; the integrand becomes d/ds[s C_j(z_s,t)]. thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative gives C_j(x,t)-0*C_j(a,t)=C_j(x,t), hence partial_j phi_C=-C_j. Therefore grad phi_C=-C with the stated finite-k and smooth joint regularity. In particular for C=e1, phi_C=-(x1-a1), so grad phi_C=-e1; the old positive integral gave +e1 and was a concrete contradiction. Neither a general non-star-shaped global existence claim nor a new physical assumption is introduced. On a ball the same construction is local even when the surrounding open set has holes; scalar circulation and vector-flux obstructions remain distinct.

J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1

items.title: Transport of flux through a moving patch
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). In the setting of [[def-em-moving-patch]], let $B$ be a $C^1$ field on a neighbourhood of the swept surface with $\operatorname{div}B=0$. Then $\Phi$ is differentiable on $I$ and $$\Phi'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r,$$ the boundary integral using the induced orientation. Without the hypothesis $\operatorname{div}B=0$ the additional term $\int_{S(t)}(v\cdot n)\,\operatorname{div}B\,dS$ appears.
items.strategy: Differentiate the parametrized flux with the parameter lemma; the area derivative contributes $\partial_uv\times r_v+r_u\times\partial_vv$, and collecting terms gives $[\partial_tB+(v\cdot\nabla)B+B\operatorname{div}v-(B\cdot\nabla)v]\cdot(r_u\times r_v)$. The published cross-product identity turns this into $[\partial_tB+v\operatorname{div}B-\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)]\cdot(r_u\times r_v)$, and patch Stokes converts the curl term into the boundary circulation. The $C^2$ hypothesis lets mixed derivatives commute. Lorentz-force interpretation is a separate physical premise.

J. Feldman, A. Rechnitzer, E. Yeager, CLP-4 Vector Calculus (UBC), §4.4 (Theorem 4.4.1)

items.title: Period averages of products of real parts of complex exponentials
items.statement: Let $\omega>0$, $T=2\pi/\omega$, and let $a,d\in\mathbb C$ (or $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, componentwise). Then $$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(a\overline d),$$ and the dot-product and cross-product versions hold componentwise. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation.
items.strategy: Write $\operatorname{Re}(z)=(z+\overline z)/2$; the product is one constant term $\frac14(a\overline d+\overline ad)$ plus oscillatory terms $e^{\pm2i\omega t}$, which integrate to zero over a full period by the fundamental theorem applied to $e^{\pm2i\omega t}/(\pm2i\omega)$.

J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1

items.title: The two-equation interface system at normal incidence
items.statement: Let $\varepsilon_j,\mu_j>0$, put $Z_j:=\sqrt{\mu_j/\varepsilon_j}$ for $j=1,2$, and let $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$ with $E_i\ne0$ satisfy the two linear equations $$E_i+E_r=E_t,\qquad \frac{E_i-E_r}{Z_1}=\frac{E_t}{Z_2}.$$ Then $E_r/E_i=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_2+Z_1)$, $E_t/E_i=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$, and $R:=\lvert E_r/E_i\rvert^2$, $T:=(Z_1/Z_2)\lvert E_t/E_i\rvert^2$ satisfy $R+T=1$. The two equations are assumed, not derived; oblique incidence, complex impedance and anisotropy require further systems and branch conventions.
items.strategy: Solve the $2\times2$ system by substitution; its determinant is $Z_1+Z_2>0$. For $R+T=1$, substitute the ratios and use $(Z_2-Z_1)^2+4Z_1Z_2=(Z_1+Z_2)^2$. No electromagnetic validity is asserted.

references.title: R. Fitzpatrick, Electromagnetism lecture notes (UT Austin), Reflection at a dielectric boundary, Eqs. (1210)-(1232)

items.title: Explicit mathematical hypothesis and convention examples for the elementary prerequisites
items.statement:
Throughout this Example and Verification, the spatial labels are local one-based names: $x_i:=x(i-1)$ for $i=1,2,3$, $e_1=(1,0,0)$, $e_2=(0,1,0)$, $e_3=(0,0,1)$, and $\partial_i$ denotes the canonical coordinate derivative $\partial_{i-1}$ under this relabeling. Thus the locally named $e_i$ has canonical coordinate $1$ at $i-1$ and $0$ at the other coordinates; the tuples, inner product, cross product, divergence and curl retain the canonical meanings of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. This local notation does not change the zero-based indices of [[lem-em-continuous-localization]].

Take the unit square $D=[0,1]^2$ as parameter region, an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, a function $a\in C^2(I)$ with $a>0$ everywhere, and

$$r(u,v,t):=\bigl(a(t)u,\ a(t)v,\ 0\bigr),\qquad B:=e_3,\qquad v(x,t):=\frac{a'(t)}{a(t)}\,(x_1,x_2,0).$$

Then $r$ is of class $C^2$ on the open set $\mathbb R^2\times I$, the tangent vectors are $r_u=(a,0,0)$ and $r_v=(0,a,0)$ with $r_u\times r_v=(0,0,a^2)\ne0$ on $D^\circ\times I^\circ=D^\circ\times I$, the field $B$ is constant with $\operatorname{div}B=0$, and $v$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3\times I$ with $v(r(u,v,t),t)=(a'(t)u,a'(t)v,0)=r_t(u,v,t)$; so the data satisfy the standing hypotheses of [[def-em-moving-patch]]. For every $t\in I$ the parametrized flux is $\Phi(t)=a(t)^2$, hence $\Phi'(t)=2a(t)a'(t)$; the fixed-time surface integral of $\partial_tB$ is $0$; and $\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)=-2(a'(t)/a(t))\,e_3$, so patch Stokes gives $\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r=-2a(t)a'(t)$, exactly the sign in the formula of [[lem-em-moving-flux]]. Dropping the term $-\oint(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$ — that is, treating the moving patch as fixed — would leave $\Phi'=0$, which the direct derivative contradicts whenever $a'(t)\ne0$. All maps are of the stated regularity and no singular support is involved; the example verifies the sign convention and the necessity of the motion term, and asserts no physical law.
items.strategy: Verify each display by direct computation at the stated regularity. The example checks the sign convention of the moving-flux lemma and the necessity of the motion term; it does not assert any physical law.

items.title: The Minkowski affine four-space: the form $\eta$, causal cones, frames and Lorentz maps
items.statement:
With $\mathbb R^4$ the space of functions $4\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-function-space]]) put $V:=\mathbb R^4$, and let $A$ be the set $\mathbb R^4$ together with the map $V\times A\to A$, $(v,p)\mapsto v+p$, given by function addition; then $(v+v')+p=v+(v'+p)$, $0+p=p$, and for all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $v+p=q$ ([[def-vector-space]]), so $A$ is an affine space with translation space $V$. Fix the ordered basis $e_0,\dots,e_3$ with $e_a(b):=1$ for $b=a$ and $0$ otherwise, and write $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ ([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). The **Minkowski form** is $\eta(v,w):=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3$; it is the standard bilinear form of [[def-standard-bilinear-form-on-a-coordinate-space]] with the sign of the first coordinate reversed and the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] on the last three coordinates, so it is a symmetric bilinear form ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]) whose matrix in $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; that matrix is invertible, so $\eta$ is nondegenerate ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]). A vector $v\ne0$ is **timelike** when $\eta(v,v)<0$, **null** when $\eta(v,v)=0$ and **spacelike** when $\eta(v,v)>0$; it is **causal** when $\eta(v,v)\le0$, and then $v^0\ne0$, so it is **future-directed** when $v^0>0$ and **past-directed** when $v^0<0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Put $C^+:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)\le0,\ v^0>0\}$ for the **future causal cone**. The **standard orientation** of $V$ is the orientation class of $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ ([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]). A **Lorentz map** is an invertible linear $L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]) with $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$; in the basis above this is exactly $M^{\mathsf T}\eta M=\eta$, where $M=[L]_{(e_0,\dots,e_3)}$, $\eta$ also denotes $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the matrix transpose is [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], by [[thm-change-of-basis-for-a-bilinear-form-is-congruence]] (a linear map preserving $\eta$ is automatically invertible because $\eta$ is nondegenerate). $L$ is **proper** when $\det L=1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and **orthochronous** when $L(C^+)=C^+$; a **frame** of $A$ is a point $o\in A$ with an ordered basis $(u_0,\dots,u_3)$ of $V$ satisfying $\eta(u_a,u_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $u_0\in C^+$, and the **coordinates** of $p\in A$ in that frame are the unique $(x^0,\dots,x^3)$ with $p=o+x^0u_0+\dots+x^3u_3$. For nonnegative integers $p,q$, a **tensor of type
$(p,q)$** on $V$ is a map $(V^*)^p\times V^q\to\mathbb R$ that is linear in
each argument separately, where $V^*$ is the algebraic dual of
[[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. An empty product is a singleton,
so a $(0,0)$ tensor is a scalar. Covectors are the $(0,1)$ case, a vector $v$
defines the $(1,0)$ tensor $\theta\mapsto\theta(v)$, and a **two-form** is a
skew-symmetric $(0,2)$ tensor. These objects are maps, with arrays recording
their components in a chosen basis.

Fix a frame $(o,(u_a))$ and define its linear coordinate map
$B:\mathbb R^4\to V$ by $B\xi:=\sum_a\xi^au_a$. It is invertible because
$(u_a)$ is a basis, and $\eta(B\xi,B\zeta)=\eta(\xi,\zeta)$ by its defining
pairings. For a Lorentz map $L:V\to V$, put $N:=[L]_{(u_a)}$, identifying
its matrix with the linear map $B^{-1}LB$ on $\mathbb R^4$. With origin fixed
and new basis $u'_a:=L^{-1}u_a$, the coordinates of the same point obey
$x'=Nx$: indeed $p-o=Bx=L^{-1}Bx'$ is equivalent to this identity.
The basis is orthonormal since $L^{-1}$ preserves $\eta$, and it is a frame
when $L$ is orthochronous, since then $L^{-1}u_0\in C^+$.

For a fixed vector $v$, covector $\theta$ and two-form $F$, let
$\widehat v:=B^{-1}v$, $\widehat\theta_a:=\theta(u_a)$ and
$\widehat F_{ab}:=F(u_a,u_b)$ be their old component columns and matrix;
primes denote the corresponding components in $(u'_a)$. Then

$$\widehat v'=N\widehat v,\qquad \widehat\theta'=(N^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\widehat\theta,\qquad \widehat F'=(N^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\widehat F N^{-1}.$$

The vector law follows from $B'=L^{-1}B=BN^{-1}$. Substituting
$u'_a=\sum_bu_b(N^{-1})^b{}_a$ into $\theta(u'_a)$ and $F(u'_a,u'_b)$ gives
the other two laws by linearity and bilinearity. Equivalently, the coordinate
functional $\theta\circ B'$ is $(\theta\circ B)\circ N^{-1}$, the transpose
operation of [[def-transpose-of-a-linear-map]], and the coordinate bilinear
form obeys $F(B'\xi,B'\zeta)=F(BN^{-1}\xi,BN^{-1}\zeta)$. The geometric
objects themselves are unchanged. In the standard frame $B=\operatorname{id}$,
$N$ is the standard coordinate matrix of $L$; in a general frame it is
$B^{-1}LB$. Finally, a fixed positive real $c$ is separate extra structure: the coordinate $x^0$ has the dimension of length and the time coordinate is $t:=x^0/c$.
items.strategy: Direct definition with the elementary verifications recorded where they belong to the definition: bilinearity and symmetry of $\eta$ from its coordinate formula, nondegeneracy from the invertible matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the implication $\eta(v,v)\le0$ and $v\ne0$ $\Rightarrow$ $v^0\ne0$ from $v^0^2\ge v^1^2+v^2^2+v^3^2$, and the matrix form $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\iff M^{\mathsf T}\eta M=\eta$ from the congruence law for the matrix of a bilinear form under a change of basis. No physical claim is made; identifying $A$ with physical spacetime and $c$ with the speed of light in vacuum is a later physical premise.

references.title: David Tong, Dynamics and Relativity, University of Cambridge Part IA Mathematical Tripos (Lent 2013), §7.1–§7.4.7, printed pp. 107–145
Sean M. Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity (arXiv:gr-qc/9712019v1), Chapter 1, printed pp. 1–30

items.title: The explicit Lorentz boost preserves $\eta$, has determinant $1$ and preserves the future cone
items.statement: Let $0\le\beta<1$ and put $\gamma:=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}>0$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). Define $\Lambda_\beta:V\to V$ by $(\Lambda_\beta v)_0=\gamma(v_0-\beta v_1)$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)_1=\gamma(v_1-\beta v_0)$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)_2=v_2$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)_3=v_3$. Then $\Lambda_\beta$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]), $\Lambda_\beta$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map, and more precisely: (a) $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$; (b) $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$; (c) $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)=C^+$; (d) $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}=\Lambda_{-\beta}$. In particular a future causal vector has future causal image and $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta v)=\eta(v,v)$ for every $v$ ([[def-real-order]], [[lem-of-square-monotone]]). The hypothesis $0\le\beta<1$ is not removable: at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined.
items.strategy: Substitution in the coordinate formula of $\eta$ gives $-\gamma^2(v_0-\beta v_1)^2+\gamma^2(v_1-\beta v_0)^2=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)(-v_0^2+v_1^2)$ with the last two coordinates unchanged, and $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$; the $0$–$1$ block of the matrix has determinant $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ and the remaining block is the identity, giving $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$; for future causal $v$ one has $|v_1|\le\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2}\le v_0$ from $\eta(v,v)\le0$, and $0\le\beta<1$ gives $(\Lambda_\beta v)_0=\gamma(v_0-\beta v_1)\ge\gamma(1-\beta)v_0>0$, so $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)\subseteq C^+$; applying the same argument to $\Lambda_{-\beta}$ and using $\Lambda_\beta\Lambda_{-\beta}=\mathrm{id}$ (again $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$) gives equality. No empirical relativity principle is proved.

references.title: David Tong, Dynamics and Relativity, University of Cambridge Part IA Mathematical Tripos (Lent 2013), §7.1–§7.4.7, printed pp. 107–145
Sean M. Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity (arXiv:gr-qc/9712019v1), Chapter 1, printed pp. 1–30

items.title: Proper time along a $C^1$ future timelike curve: strictly increasing reparametrization with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$
items.statement: Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $z:J\to\mathbb R^4$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $\eta(z'(s),z'(s))<0$ and $z^0{}'(s)>0$ for every $s\in J$; $z'$ is the derivative of the vector-valued curve ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) and such a $z$ is called a $C^1$ future timelike curve. Put $g(s):=-\eta(z'(s),z'(s))>0$, fix $s_0\in J$, and define $\tau(s):=c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{g(u)}\,du$ for $s\in J$. Then: (1) $g$ is continuous on $J$ and so is $s\mapsto\sqrt{g(s)}$, where $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is the nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); (2) $\tau$ is differentiable on $J$ with $\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{g(s)}>0$, hence $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $J$, injective, and continuous ([[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]], [[thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative]]); (3) the inverse $\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to J$ is differentiable at every point $\tau(s)$ of the interval $\tau[J]$, with $(\tau^{-1})'(\tau(s))=c/\sqrt{g(s)}$ ([[thm-continuous-inverse]], [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]]); (4) the reparametrized curve $z\circ\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to\mathbb R^4$ is differentiable at every $\tau(s)$, with tangent $U(\tau(s)):=c\,z'(s)/\sqrt{g(s)}$ satisfying $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ ([[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]); (5) if instead $\eta(z'(s),z'(s))=0$ for all $s\in J$, then $g=0$, $\tau\equiv0$ on $J$ and $\tau$ is not injective, so a null curve carries no proper-time parametrization ([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]); (6) if $z(s)=p+sv$ with $\eta(v,v)<0$ and $v_0>0$, then $\tau(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}\,(s-s_0)$ and $U=c\,v/\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}$ is constant ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], [[def-derivative]]). The identification of such straight lines with inertial motion is a physical premise and is not asserted here.
items.strategy: $C^1$ gives continuity of the components $z^a{}'$ and [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] passes between the vector-valued and component statements; the four squares $(z^a{}')^2$ and their signed sum are continuous by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $g$ is continuous; $\sqrt g$ is continuous because squaring is a continuous injection of $[0,\infty)$ onto itself with continuous inverse $\sqrt{\cdot}$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]], [[thm-continuous-inverse]]), and composition preserves continuity. [[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]] makes $\tau$ a primitive of the continuous function $c^{-1}\sqrt g$ on $J$, giving (2) with [[thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative]]; [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]] (hypotheses: $\tau$ continuous and injective on the interval $J$, $\tau'(s)\ne0$) gives (3); [[thm-chain-rule]] applied to the components of $z\circ\tau^{-1}$ and reassembled gives (4), where $\eta(U,U)=(c^2/g)\eta(z',z')=-c^2$ uses bilinearity and symmetry of $\eta$; (5) is the zero integrand case; (6) is direct computation with constant $z'=v$.

references.title: David Tong, Dynamics and Relativity, University of Cambridge Part IA Mathematical Tripos (Lent 2013), §7.1–§7.4.7, printed pp. 107–145
Sean M. Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity (arXiv:gr-qc/9712019v1), Chapter 1, printed pp. 1–30

items.title: Antisymmetric contractions vanish and $mU'=q\Phi(U)$ preserves $\eta(U,U)$
items.statement:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be the four-dimensional real Minkowski vector space of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]], with the fixed form of signature $(-1,1,1,1)$. Let $F:V	imes V	o\mathbb R$ be a skew-symmetric bilinear form, $F(u,v)=-F(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in V$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Since $\eta$ is nondegenerate, for each $u\in V$ there is exactly one $\Phi(u)\in V$ with $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w\in V$ ([[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]], [[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and $\Phi:V	o V$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]); with $F_{\alpha eta}:=F(e_\alpha,e_ eta)$ in a frame $\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha eta}u^ eta$, the index-raised form of $F$. Then $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$ for every $u\in V$; in components $u_\mu F^\mu{}_
u u^
u=0$. Consequently, if $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), $U:J	o V$ is differentiable ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and $m\,U'(s)=q\,\Phi(U(s))$ on $J$ for some real $m
e0$ and $q$, then $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on $J$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]). The same norm-conservation conclusion holds for a family of skew forms $F_s$ and their pointwise operators $\Phi_s$ defined by $\eta(\Phi_s(u),w)=F_s(w,u)$, when $mU'(s)=q\Phi_s(U(s))$: no derivative of $F_s$ is required. In particular one may evaluate a varying field $F_x$ along a differentiable trajectory $x(s)$. This is a conditional statement about the given equation; it does not assert that this equation governs any particle.
items.strategy: For each $u$, $w\mapsto F(w,u)$ is a linear functional. The nondegenerate finite-dimensional form $\eta$ identifies $V$ with $V^*$, so it gives a unique $\Phi(u)$; bilinearity and uniqueness make $\Phi$ linear. In a frame, evaluating the defining pairing at $w=e_\alpha$ gives $\eta_{\alpha\mu}\Phi(u)^\mu=F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$, hence $\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$. Taking $w=u$ gives $\eta(\Phi(u),u)=F(u,u)=0$ by skew-symmetry, and symmetry of $\eta$ gives $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$. For the norm claim $f(s):=\eta(U(s),U(s))=\sum_a\epsilon_a(U^a(s))^2$, with $\epsilon=(-1,1,1,1)$, satisfies $f'=2\eta(U,U')$ by the product rule. The equation gives $\eta(U,U')=(q/m)\eta(U,\Phi(U))=0$, so the zero-derivative theorem on the open interval $J$ makes $f$ constant. The identical pointwise calculation with $\Phi_s$ proves the varying-form clause: differentiate $\eta(U,U)$ only, not $F_s$ or $\Phi_s$. No constant-field assumption is used in that clause.

references.title: David Tong, Dynamics and Relativity, University of Cambridge Part IA Mathematical Tripos (Lent 2013), §7.1–§7.4.7, printed pp. 107–145
Sean M. Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity (arXiv:gr-qc/9712019v1), Chapter 1, printed pp. 1–30

items.title: Explicit mathematical hypothesis/convention examples
items.statement:
With $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: (i) the vector $v$ with components
$(1,0,0,0)$ is future timelike and unit, $\eta(v,v)=-1$. (ii) For $0<\beta<1$
the boost $\Lambda_\beta$ of
[[lem-em-boost-preserves-metric]] sends $v$ to the vector with components
$(\gamma,-\gamma\beta,0,0)$,
whose quadratic value $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta v)$ is
$-\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=-1$ and whose time component
$\gamma$ is positive; at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined, so the
hypothesis $0\le\beta<1$ cannot be dropped. (iii) The null line
$z(s)=(s,s,0,0)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, has $\eta(z',z')=0$, so the proper-time
construction of [[lem-em-proper-time-reparametrization]] gives $\tau\equiv0$,
which is not an invertible parameter: the timelike hypothesis cannot be weakened
to causal. (iv) For the symmetric nonzero form $F:=\eta$ one has
$\Phi=\mathrm{id}$ and $\eta(v,\Phi(v))=\eta(v,v)=-1\ne0$, so the antisymmetry
hypothesis of [[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]] is genuine. (v) For
the skew form with $F_{01}=1$, $F_{10}=-1$ and other coefficients zero, the
operator of [[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]] sends $e_0$ to $-e_1$:
$\eta(-e_1,w)=-w^1=F(w,e_0)$. Thus its invariant pairing and standard
raised-index formula have the same sign, and $\eta(e_0,\Phi(e_0))=0$. No
physical clock premise or experimental claim is used.
items.strategy: Five direct computations in the fixed standard frame: evaluation of $\eta$ on the given vectors, substitution of $v$ in the boost formula, the vanishing of the null tangent, and the identification $\Phi=\mathrm{id}$ when $F=\eta$ (uniqueness in the defining property of $\Phi$). For (v), the first column of $\eta^{-1}F$ is $(0,-1,0,0)$; both pairings equal $-w^1$, and the time-space orthogonality is immediate. All are exact finite computations; no source or physical assumption is needed.

items.title: The fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations for continuous coefficients
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be continuous. If $\int_U\langle g,h\rangle\,d\lambda=0$ for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^m)$, then $g=0$ on $U$. Here $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product and $\int_U\langle g,h\rangle\,d\lambda$ is the finite sum $\sum_{i<m}\int_U g_ih_i\,d\lambda$ of integrals of continuous compactly supported functions ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). The scalar case is $m=1$: a continuous $g$ with $\int_Ugh\,d\lambda=0$ for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ vanishes on $U$. The vector case is deduced from the scalar case componentwise, each component tested separately. The conclusion is pointwise on $U$, and the hypothesis is the full family of compactly supported smooth test functions. The Axiom of Countable Choice is declared because the localization lemma [[lem-em-continuous-localization]] and the measurability fact [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]] used in the recorded proof assume it; no other choice principle enters.
items.strategy:
Scalar case. Suppose $g(p)
e0$ for some $p\in U$; replacing $g$ by $-g$, which satisfies the same hypothesis, assume $g(p)>0$. Openness of $U$ and continuity of $g$ at $p$ give $r>0$ with $B(p,r)\subseteq U$ and $g\ge g(p)/2$ on $B(p,r)$. Apply the cutoff lemma to the compact set $\{p\}$ inside the open ball $B(p,r)$: it yields $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B(p,r))$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighbourhood of $p$, so $\chi(p)=1$ and $\chi$ extends by zero to a test function in $C_c^\infty(U)$. Then $\varphi:=g\chi$ is continuous on $U$ as a product of continuous real functions, satisfies $\varphi\ge0$ because $g>0$ on the support of $\chi$, and has $\varphi(p)=g(p)>0$, so $\varphi
e0$. Were $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda=0$: the localization lemma applied to the continuous function $\varphi$ (contrapositive form of [[lem-em-continuous-localization]]) produces a ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$ with $\int_V\varphi\,d\lambda
e0$; since $\varphi\ge0$ this integral is positive, and monotonicity of the nonnegative integral gives $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda\ge\int_V\varphi\,d\lambda>0$, contradicting $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda=0$. But $\chi$ is an admissible test function, so the hypothesis gives $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda=\int_U g\chi\,d\lambda=0$; hence no point $p$ with $g(p)
e0$ exists. Vector case. For each $i<m$ and each $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$, apply the hypothesis to $h=\psi e_i$ to get $\int_U g_i\psi\,d\lambda=0$; the scalar case gives $g_i=0$. Measurability of $\varphi$ comes from continuity, and the positive-integral comparison uses the order rules for the nonnegative integral. Continuity is retained verbatim: a measurable $g$ that is $0$ almost everywhere but not everywhere passes every test pairing without being the zero function, so the pointwise conclusion genuinely uses continuity.

items.title: Compact variations of the quadratic field functional: first variation and the coefficient equation
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be a bounded open set, let $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be an open neighbourhood of its closure, let $\kappa>0$, and let $A:N	o V=\mathbb R^4$ and $J:N	o V$ be smooth ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Use the Minkowski form $\eta$ and the index conventions of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]]: $A^\mu$ denotes the components of $A$ in the standard basis, $A_
u:=\eta_{
u\mu}A^\mu$, $F_{\mu
u}:=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu$, $F^{\mu
u}:=\eta^{\mu\alpha}\eta^{
u eta}F_{\alpha eta}$, and $J^
u A_
u$ is the indicated contraction of the components of $J$ with the covector $A_
u$. Put $L:=- rac{1}{4\kappa}F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}+J^
u A_
u$ and $S[A]:=\int_U L\,d\lambda$, the $4$-dimensional Lebesgue integral of $L$ over $U$. Then $S[A]$ is a finite real number, and for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;V)$, with $h_
u:=\eta_{
u\mu}h^\mu$ and $G_{\mu
u}:=\partial_\mu h_
u-\partial_
u h_\mu$: (a) the map $s\mapsto S[A+sh]$ is the quadratic polynomial $S[A]+s\int_U\ell_1\,d\lambda+s^2\int_U\ell_2\,d\lambda$, where $\ell_1:=-\kappa^{-1}F^{\mu
u}\partial_\mu h_
u+J^
u h_
u$ and $\ell_2:=- rac{1}{4\kappa}G_{\mu
u}G^{\mu
u}$, so that its derivative at $s=0$ is $\int_U igl(-\kappa^{-1}F^{\mu
u}\partial_\mu h_
u+J^
u h_
u igr)d\lambda$; (b) that first variation also equals $\int_U igl(\kappa^{-1}\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}+J^
u igr)h_
u\,d\lambda$; (c) $A$ is stationary for $S$, meaning that the derivative in (a) vanishes for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;V)$, if and only if $\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=-\kappa J^
u$ for every $
u$ on $U$, all derivatives being classical partial derivatives of the smooth field $A$. This is a pure mathematical statement about the functional $S$: existence of a stationary field $A$ is not asserted, and identifying $\kappa$ with the vacuum permeability, $A$ with a physical potential or $S$ with a physical action is a later physical model choice.
items.strategy:
Well-definedness. Write also $h$ for its extension by zero to $N$; that extension is smooth because the compact support of $h$ has positive distance from the complement of the open $U$, so $A+sh$ is smooth on $N$ and $S[A+sh]$ is defined for every real $s$. Expansion. For each $s$ one has $F_{\mu
u}(s)=F_{\mu
u}+sG_{\mu
u}$ by linearity of the partial derivatives in the variation. Bilinearity of $\eta$ gives $F_{\mu
u}(s)F^{\mu
u}(s)=F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}+2sF^{\mu
u}G_{\mu
u}+s^2G_{\mu
u}G^{\mu
u}$; the split $G_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu h_
u-\partial_
u h_\mu$ and the antisymmetry $F^{\mu
u}=-F^{
u\mu}$ give $F^{\mu
u}G_{\mu
u}=2F^{\mu
u}\partial_\mu h_
u$ (the two terms are equal after relabelling). Hence $L(A+sh)=L(A)+s\ell_1+s^2\ell_2$ pointwise on $N$ with the displayed $\ell_1,\ell_2$. The functions $L(A),\ell_1,\ell_2$ are continuous on the compact set $\overline U$, hence bounded, and the bounded open $U$ lies in a box of finite Lebesgue measure, so all three are integrable on $U$; linearity of the integral in $s$ gives the polynomial identity in (a) and, by differentiating the polynomial, the displayed derivative, with no exchange of limit and integral. Conversion. Fix $
u$. The function $x\mapsto F^{\mu
u}(x)$ (sum over $\mu$, with the repeated-index convention) is of class $C^1$ on the open set $U$, so by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]] its classical partial derivative $\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}$ is its weak derivative; the test identity of [[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] with the test function $h_

u}\partial_\mu h_
u\,d\lambda=-\int_U(\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u})h_
u\,d\lambda$. Substituting this into (a) yields (b). No boundary term remains precisely because $h$ is compactly supported in $U$; for a non-compactly-supported variation the identity fails, as the B example records. Coefficient equation. Put $C^
u:=\kappa^{-1}\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}+J^
u$, a continuous coefficient array on $U$. By (b) the first variation is $\int_U\sum_
u C^

u\mu}h^\mu$. Set $k_

u}k_

Thus stationarity is exactly vanishing of the Euclidean pairing of the numeric array $(C^0,C^1,C^2,C^3)$ with every numeric test tuple $(k_0,k_1,k_2,k_3)$, not an identification of the original contravariant $h$ with its lowered array. The vector clause of [[lem-em-fundamental-variation-lemma]] therefore gives $C^

The Axiom of Countable Choice is used exactly through [[lem-em-fundamental-variation-lemma]] and [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]]; the expansion step uses none.

items.title: Bounded-error model comparison: a derivative lower bound confines compatible parameters
items.statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), let $\theta_0\in I$, and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ on $I$ in the sense that $f$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ and $f'$ is continuous on $I$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]). Assume $f(\theta_0)=0$ and that $f'(\theta)\ge m>0$ for every $\theta\in I$. Let a recorded scalar $\hat y\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\hat y|\le s$ with $s\ge0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), and let a separately specified calibration-error model bound be $|y-\hat y|\le\delta$ with $\delta\ge0$ for a value $y$ assigned to the same quantity. If a model requires $y=f(\theta)$ for some $\theta\in I$, then every $\theta\in I$ compatible with those two simultaneous bounds satisfies $$|\theta-\theta_0|\le\frac{s+\delta}{m};$$ equivalently, if a proposed $\theta$ violates this bound, then the specified model-plus-error-bound pair is incompatible with the premises. The conclusion is a deterministic conditional statement about the stated bounds; it is not a sampling law, a statistical inference, or a claim about the historical reports of the causal-response page.
items.strategy: The triangle inequality for the absolute value ([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[def-abs-value]]) gives $|y|\le|\hat y|+|y-\hat y|\le s+\delta$. For $\theta\ne\theta_0$ apply the mean value theorem ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]) to $f$ on the closed interval with endpoints $\theta$ and $\theta_0$ (an interval contained in $I$ by order convexity, [[def-interval]]): there is $\xi$ strictly between them with $f(\theta)-f(\theta_0)=f'(\xi)(\theta-\theta_0)$, hence $|f(\theta)|\ge m|\theta-\theta_0|$ because $f(\theta_0)=0$ and $f'\ge m>0$. Combining $|f(\theta)|=|y|\le s+\delta$ with the lower bound and dividing by $m>0$ gives the stated bound; $\theta=\theta_0$ is immediate. Differentiability of $f$ everywhere and continuity of $f'$ on $I$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]) are used to make $f$ continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on its interior, exactly the mean-value hypotheses.

items.title: Legendre polynomials from a convergent zonal kernel: generating function and exterior expansion
items.statement:
For $z\in[-1,1]$ define the real polynomial $P_l(z)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi\bigl[z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\,\cos\theta\bigr]^l\,d\theta$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$. Then $P_l$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $l$ with $|P_l(z)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, $P_l(1)=1$, and for $|q|<1$ the series $\sum_{l\ge0}q^lP_l(z)$ converges absolutely and uniformly on $[-1,1]$ with

$$(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}q^lP_l(z),$$

where the branch is the analytic square root equal to $1$ at $q=0$ ([[def-series-of-real-functions]], [[thm-weierstrass-m-test-for-function-series]]). Consequently, for $x\ne0$, $r:=|x|>|y|$ and $n=x/|x|$ and $N\in\mathbb N_0$,

$$\bigl|\,|x-y|^{-1}-\sum_{l=0}^{N}|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(n\cdot y/|y|)\bigr|\le|y|^{N+1}|x|^{-N-2}(1-|y|/|x|)^{-1},$$

uniformly on $|y|\le a<r$ (with $y=0$ interpreted by the zero higher terms), and after integrating against an $L^1$ source the corresponding multipole expansion converges with that error times its $L^1$ norm. For the integrated $L^1$-source and every-spatial-derivative assertions, assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) through the Lebesgue and harmonic-estimate interfaces. On an observation compact set disjoint from $\overline{B_a(0)}$ every fixed spatial derivative series converges uniformly, uniformly also over $|y|\le a$, by harmonicity of the coefficient terms and [[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]]. The initial finite-Riemann polynomial/generating assertions are choice-free. This lemma supplies the convergent zonal kernel; it does not by itself prove a spherical $L^2$ basis or boundary convergence.
items.strategy:
Expand the finite power in the defining Riemann integral: odd cosine powers integrate to zero by the substitution theta to pi-theta, and even powers have factors $(1-z^2)^jz^{l-2j}$, so $P_l$ is a real polynomial, with $P_l(1)=1$ and $|P_l(z)|\le1$. For each FIXED real $z\in[-1,1]$, put $w(\theta)=z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta$; $|w|\le1$, so the geometric series is uniformly convergent on every $|q|\le q_0<1$ and finite-Riemann termwise integration gives $G_z(q)=\sum_lq^lP_l(z)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi(1-qw(\theta))^{-1}d\theta$. The sum is holomorphic on the unit disk by [[thm-termwise-differentiation-of-complex-power-series]]. No holomorphy in z at the endpoints is asserted.

For real $a>|b|$ the tangent substitution gives $I(a,b)=\int_0^\pi(a+b\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\pi/\sqrt{a^2-b^2}$ by [[thm-substitution]] and [[thm-principal-inverse-tangent-calculus]]. Near $(a,b)=(1,0)$ the rational integrand and its first parameter derivatives are uniformly bounded on the compact theta interval, so uniform difference quotients through the finite Riemann integral give holomorphy in each parameter separately. The identity $I(a,b)^2(a^2-b^2)=\pi^2$ first extends in complex a for every fixed small real b, then in complex b for every fixed nearby complex a, by the ONE-variable [[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]]. Substitute $a=1-qz$, $b=-iq\sqrt{1-z^2}$ near q0 to get $(1-2qz+q^2)G_z(q)^2=1$. This holomorphic identity extends over the connected unit disk by the same one-variable theorem. Since $G_z(0)=1$, it is exactly the specified analytic inverse-square-root branch. The zeros of the polynomial factor lie on the unit circle for every fixed real z. Substitution q=|y|/r now proves the exterior kernel series and its geometric remainder, including zero y.

Each coefficient $c_l(x,y)=|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l((x/|x|)\cdot(y/|y|))$ is smooth and harmonic in x away from zero. Indeed it equals $1/l!$ times the lth t-derivative at t0 of $|x-ty|^{-1}$, by the proved scalar power series and [[cor-complex-power-series-coefficient-formula]]. On a neighbourhood of any fixed x nonzero and t0 this kernel is smooth and harmonic in x by [[lem-laplace-fundamental-solution-is-harmonic-off-its-pole]]; finite mixed derivative commutation [[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]] makes its t-coefficient harmonic. The corresponding degree-l solid polynomial in y is harmonic in y by the same argument, using $\Delta_y|x-ty|^{-1}=0$ for all sufficiently small real t. This also supplies the solid-harmonic coefficient used by the later addition lemma without a cyclic dependence.

The empty observation compact has a vacuous uniform-convergence claim. Otherwise fix a nonempty compact observation set K with inf_K|x|>a. Choose a positive delta and a bounded closed neighbourhood Kplus of K with every closed delta-ball centred on K contained in Kplus and inf_Kplus|x|>a. The geometric kernel estimate gives a uniform tail bound E_N tending to zero on Kplus times the whole closed source ball |y|<=a. Harmonic partial-sum differences v satisfy the exact [[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]] bound $|D^\alpha v(x)|\le C_{3,\alpha}\delta^{-3-|\alpha|}\int_{B_\delta(x)}|v|\le C_{3,\alpha}\delta^{-3-|\alpha|}|B_\delta|\sup_{Kplus}|v|$. Thus every spatial derivative is uniformly Cauchy on K, uniformly in y. Uniform derivative limits are identified inductively along short coordinate segments by [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], so they are exactly the derivatives of the kernel. Against a compact $L^1$ density, the same bound times |rho| gives an integrable envelope and multiplies each tail by ||rho||1 using [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]. Countable Choice enters only the Lebesgue and harmonic-estimate branches; the initial finite polynomial and scalar generating argument uses no Choice. No multivariable complex Cauchy estimate is invoked. For an actual L1 source choose its representative zero outside the closed source ball. On each small open observation-coordinate interval inside Kplus, every kernel derivative is smooth on the fixed compact source ball and has a uniform finite bound C_alpha; the next derivative integrand is bounded by C_alpha times |rho|, an integrable majorant. Thus [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applies with zero exceptional set after the off-ball integrand is defined as zero. This identifies all integral derivatives directly as well as by the uniform harmonic-series limit.

references.locator: Full260-page author PDF retrieved and relevant Chapter5 sections inspected: printed78-82 (orthogonal spherical decomposition),94-100 (zonal harmonic projection/addition/Poisson expansion). The source uses unit-mass sphere measure; formulas here adapt to mass4pi.
