items.title: Constrained smooth vacuum Maxwell initial-value theory, finite-energy conservation and finite propagation
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
[[def-countable-choice]]), inherited from
[[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]]. Let $t_0<T$ be real, let
$E_0,B_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^\infty$ fields
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) on the whole-space laboratory
region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the
constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and assume the constraints
$$\operatorname{div}E_0=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B_0=0$$ on $\mathbb R^3$
([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Put
$\dot E_0:=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$ and
$\dot B_0:=-\operatorname{curl}E_0$. No decay, boundedness, compactness or
finite-energy hypothesis is imposed on the data. Then:

(a) [Existence and explicit representation] There are jointly $C^\infty$
fields $E,B:\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R^3$ (in the extension sense of
[[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]]) satisfying the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$,
$J\equiv0$ and the initial conditions $E(\cdot,t_0)=E_0$,
$B(\cdot,t_0)=B_0$, $\partial_tE(\cdot,t_0)=\dot E_0$,
$\partial_tB(\cdot,t_0)=\dot B_0$. Explicitly, each component $E_i$ is the
scalar solution $u$ of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](a) with data
$(a,b)=(E_{0,i},\dot E_{0,i})$ and $h=0$, each $B_i$ that with
$(a,b)=(B_{0,i},\dot B_{0,i})$, in the spherical-mean representation
$u=\partial_sH_a+H_b$ of that theorem, the mean being that of
[[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]].

(b) [Uniqueness] Every pair of jointly $C^2$ fields on
$\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ (in the extension sense) satisfying the same four
equations with $\rho\equiv0$, $J\equiv0$ and $E'(\cdot,t_0)=E_0$,
$B'(\cdot,t_0)=B_0$ equals $(E,B)$; the time derivatives at $t_0$ are then
automatically $\dot E_0,\dot B_0$ by the Ampere and Faraday equations.

(c) [Finite propagation and domain of dependence] If second constrained data
$(E_0',B_0')$ agree with $(E_0,B_0)$ together with all curls on the closed ball
$\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$ — that is, $E_0=E_0'$, $B_0=B_0'$,
$\operatorname{curl}E_0=\operatorname{curl}E_0'$ and
$\operatorname{curl}B_0=\operatorname{curl}B_0'$ there — then the
corresponding solutions agree at $(x_*,t_*)$, for all $x_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and
$t_*\in[t_0,T]$. Consequently the value at $(x_*,t_*)$ is determined by the
Cauchy data on the closed backward cone
$K(x_*,t_*)=\{(y,v):t_0\le v\le t_*,\ |y-x_*|\le c(t_*-v)\}$ of
[[def-forward-and-backward-wave-cones-domain-of-dependence-and-influence]]. In
the causal geometry of the adopted affine Minkowski model this cone is the
intersection of the slab with the model's causal past of the event $(x_*,t_*)$ in the chart $x^0=ct$; by
the reachability objects of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]] and the
straight-segment criterion and time monotonicity of
[[thm-sr-future-cone-and-flat-domain-of-dependence]], events in the slab outside it cannot
be joined to $(x_*,t_*)$ by a future causal path, so the constructed field
supplies no vacuum influence outside the model's causal cones; this
identification of the PDE cone with the model's causal cone is the modelling
statement of the item, not an additional empirical claim.

(d) [Compact support] If in addition $E_0$ and $B_0$ vanish off a compact set
$K\subset\mathbb R^3$, choose $\rho>0$ with $K\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]); then for every $t\in[t_0,T]$ one has
$E(x,t)=B(x,t)=0$ whenever $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$.

(e) [Finite-energy branch] Define
$u(x,t)=(\varepsilon_0|E(x,t)|^2+\mu_0^{-1}|B(x,t)|^2)/2$ and
$S=\mu_0^{-1}E\times B$ as in [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and define total
energy by the nonnegative ball exhaustion
$\mathcal E(t):=\sup_{R>0}\int_{B_R(0)}u(x,t)\,dx\in[0,\infty]$. If
$\mathcal E(t_0)<\infty$, then $\mathcal E(t)=\mathcal E(t_0)$ for every
$t\in[t_0,T]$. More locally, for every $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, $r>0$ and
$t_0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\int_{B_r(x_0)}u(x,t)\,dx\le\int_{B_{r+c(t-s)}(x_0)}u(x,s)\,dx.$$
This is a branch for the same smooth constrained data with finite initial
energy; no existence result for nonsmooth finite-energy data is asserted.

(f) [Scope] This is the smooth whole-space vacuum branch with initially
constraint-satisfying data; general smooth non-decaying data may have infinite
total energy, and no boundary condition, inhomogeneous source, weak-branch
content or empirical claim is asserted. The result is conditional on the
adopted postulates and on $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the latter used through the
scalar theorem and the divergence and substitution suppliers in clause (e).
items.strategy: Set $\dot E_0=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$, $\dot B_0=-\operatorname{curl}E_0$, and solve the six scalar Cauchy problems by [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](a) with data $(E_{0,i},\dot E_{0,i})$ and $(B_{0,i},\dot B_{0,i})$; the $C^\infty$ claim and the explicit representation through the spherical-mean family $H_\varphi=sM_{cs}\varphi$ are clause (a) of that theorem, whose mean is that of [[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]]. Put $R_i:=\partial_tE_i-c^2(\operatorname{curl}B)_i$ and $Q_i:=\partial_tB_i+(\operatorname{curl}E)_i$. Each is $C^\infty$ and solves the homogeneous scalar wave equation: differentiating the component wave equations and commuting derivatives ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]) gives $\partial_t^2R_i=c^2\Delta R_i$, $\partial_t^2Q_i=c^2\Delta Q_i$. Initially $R=Q=0$, and $\partial_tR_i(t_0)=c^2\Delta E_{0,i}+c^2(\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E_0)_i=c^2\nabla_i\operatorname{div}E_0=0$, $\partial_tQ_i(t_0)=c^2\nabla_i\operatorname{div}B_0=0$ by the curl-curl identity [[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]] and the constraints. The uniqueness clause [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](b) applied to the zero wave problem gives $R=Q=0$, i.e. the two evolution equations. The constructed fields are smooth and satisfy the evolution equations with $\operatorname{div}E(\cdot,t_0)=\operatorname{div}E_0=0$ and $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t_0)=0$, so the constraint propagation of [[pthm-em-gauss-constraint-propagation]](a) with $\rho=J=0$ gives $\operatorname{div}E\equiv\operatorname{div}B\equiv0$; all four Maxwell equations therefore hold. Uniqueness (b): any other $C^2$ solution has componentwise the same Cauchy data and, by [[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]], satisfies the homogeneous scalar wave equation, so [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](b) identifies it with the constructed field. Clause (c) applies [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](c) componentwise, whose hypothesis is agreement of both scalar data functions on the ball: $E_0$ and $c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$ for the $E$ components, $B_0$ and $-\operatorname{curl}E_0$ for the $B$ components, exactly the stated hypothesis; the cone reformulation uses the backward-cone object and the causal reachability and future-causal-path conclusions of the two cited SR items as the model's geometric language. Clause (d) applies [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](d) to each component, whose data vanish off $K$ because $E_0,B_0$ and their curls do. For (e), the local source-free Poynting identity [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]](a) is $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=0$. The coordinate identity $|E\times B|^2=|E|^2|B|^2-(E\cdot B)^2$ (by expansion of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]) gives $|E\times B|\le|E||B|$. This and $2pq\le p^2+q^2$, applied to $p=\sqrt{\varepsilon_0}|E|$, $q=|B|/\sqrt{\mu_0}$, give $|S|\le cu$. For a positive $C^1$ radius $r(v)$ put $F(v)=\int_{B_{r(v)}(x_0)}u(x,v)\,dx$. To justify moving-ball differentiation, set $x=x_0+r(v)y$ in the integral using [[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]]; the result is $r(v)^3\int_{B_1}u(x_0+r(v)y,v)\,dy$. One may replace $B_1$ by its compact closure because its boundary is Lebesgue null by [[lem-unit-sphere-is-lebesgue-null]]; translated scaled spheres are likewise null by the substitution lemma. [[lem-em-parameter-integrals]] differentiates this fixed compact integral. The radius terms are $(r'/r)\int_{B_r}\operatorname{div}((x-x_0)u)\,dx$, which by [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]] equal $r'\int_{\partial B_r}u\,dS$; the time term, by the same divergence theorem and Poynting, is $-\int_{\partial B_r}S\cdot n\,dS$. Thus $F'(v)=-\int_{\partial B_{r(v)}}(S\cdot n-r'(v)u)\,dS$. Choosing $r(v)=r+c(t-v)$ gives $F'=-\int_{\partial B_{r(v)}}(S\cdot n+cu)\,dS\le0$ by $|S|\le cu$, and integrating gives the stated local estimate. Taking the supremum in $r$ yields $\mathcal E(t)\le\mathcal E(s)$. For the reverse inequality apply the same local argument to the smooth source-free pair $\widetilde E(x,v)=E(x,t-v)$, $\widetilde B(x,v)=-B(x,t-v)$ for $0\le v\le t-s$. Its Maxwell equations follow by direct differentiation, its energy is $u(x,t-v)$ and its flux is $-S(x,t-v)$, so $\mathcal E(s)\le\mathcal E(t)$. This proves equality and finite-energy preservation when initially finite. Applied to the difference of two smooth source-free Maxwell solutions (the equations subtract), the same local estimate yields an energy uniqueness proof: zero initial difference has zero energy on every later ball; its continuous nonnegative density is zero everywhere, so both difference fields vanish. This supplements the scalar uniqueness argument without restricting its arbitrary-growth conclusion. All ball closures are compact smooth domains and the integrands are smooth; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used through the divergence/substitution suppliers as well as the scalar theorem. The arbitrary-growth branch requires no decay or additional regularity. Apply Gauss propagation on the open slab and use endpoint continuity. The causal-past assertion concerns only the slab intersection. Signed substitutions use finite positive and negative parts.
items.physical_scope: Conditional whole-space smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell initial-value theory in a named inertial chart with SI constants: existence, uniqueness, finite propagation speed $c$, compact-support propagation and smooth finite-energy conservation for initially constraint-satisfying $C^\infty$ data of arbitrary growth. Excluded: nonsmooth and weak-branch data, sources, boundary conditions, finite-domain problems, nonsmooth finite-energy data, and any empirical claim. Smooth finite-energy initial data retain their total energy; arbitrary-growth data remain allowed. $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is declared and used through the scalar wave theorem and clause (e)'s divergence and substitution suppliers.

items.title: Period-averaged energy density, Poynting vector and momentum flux of a plane wave
items.statement:
Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ with $\omega=c|k|$, let
$e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$, and let $(E,B)$ be
the corresponding plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Let $u$ and
$S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and $g=S/c^2$, $\sigma$, $\Pi=-\sigma$ the
momentum density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Write $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|e|^2=e\cdot\overline e$, $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle f\rangle:=\frac1T\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ be the period average at fixed
$x$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$:

(a) [Averaged energy density] $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$,
independent of $x$ and of the starting time.

(b) [Averaged Poynting vector]
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$; hence
$\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$, and the period-averaged intensity
is $I:=|\langle S\rangle|=c\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2$.

(c) [Averaged momentum density, stress and momentum flux]
$\langle g\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2c}|e|^2\hat k$, and componentwise
$\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$, equivalently
$\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$; the period-averaged
momentum flux across a plane with unit normal $n$ (with the physical balance
interpretation conditional as in (d)) is therefore
$\langle u\rangle(\hat k\cdot n)\hat k$, a pure flux along $\hat k$ with signed
coefficient $(I/c)(\hat k\cdot n)$ and magnitude $(I/c)|\hat k\cdot n|$. The
tensor identity holds for every complex transverse amplitude $e$, not only for
real or circular ones.

(d) [Balance reading with continuum coupling] For this clause additionally
adopt [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](ii) for the empty-matter model on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: the matter energy density
$w:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, energy flux
$Q:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, momentum density
$p:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ and momentum flux
$P:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ are all identically
zero, as are the source fields $\rho,J$. The adopted electromagnetic force
and power densities are then $f:=\rho E+J\times B=0$ and $J\cdot E=0$,
respectively; the zero matter balances are satisfied. Under this additional
interpretation premise the local identities of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]]
and [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]] hold for this field; since $u,g,S,\sigma$ are $T$-periodic in $t$, the period averages of
their time derivatives vanish ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), so averaging the
identities gives $\operatorname{div}\langle S\rangle=0$ and
$\operatorname{div}\langle\sigma\rangle=0$ consistently (both averaged fields
are in fact constant), and the reading of $u,S,g,\Pi$ as energy and momentum
densities and fluxes is that of those two theorems.

(e) [Scope] These are exact identities for the ideal plane wave; $I$ is the
intensity used by the radiation-pressure thought experiment of the companion
page and in radiation-flux arguments. No detection statistics, no finite-beam
or finite-time realisation and no empirical claim is made, and the zero
amplitude gives the zero wave and zero total energy, whereas every nonzero
amplitude gives infinite total energy over $\mathbb R^3$.
items.strategy: Clause (a)-(c) are the compact-period calculation of [[lem-em-period-average]] applied componentwise: with $E=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{i\theta})$, $B=\operatorname{Re}(b\,e^{i\theta})$, $\theta=k\cdot x-\omega t$, the lemma gives $\langle E_iE_j\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})$, $\langle B_iB_j\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(b_i\overline{b_j})$ and $\langle(E\times B)_i\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}((e\times\overline b)_i)$; hence $\langle|E|^2\rangle=|e|^2/2$ and, using $b=k\times e/\omega$ and $|k|=\omega/c$, $\langle|B|^2\rangle=|b|^2/2=|e|^2/(2c^2)$. Substituting into $u$ and $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] and using $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\varepsilon_0$ gives (a) and (b), since $e\times\overline b=e\times(k\times\overline e)/\omega=k|e|^2/\omega$ by the cross-product identity of [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]] and $e\cdot k=0$. For (c), expand $\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=(\varepsilon_0/2)\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})-(\varepsilon_0/4)\delta_{ij}|e|^2+(1/(2\mu_0))\operatorname{Re}(b_i\overline{b_j})-(1/(4\mu_0))\delta_{ij}|b|^2$ and substitute $b_i\overline{b_j}=(k\times e)_i\overline{(k\times e)_j}/\omega^2$ together with the coordinate identity $(k\times e)_i\overline{(k\times e)_j}=|k|^2|e|^2\delta_{ij}-k_ik_j|e|^2-|k|^2\overline{e_i}e_j$ (a bilinear coordinate expansion of the cross product, again from the cited lemma); with $|k|^2/\omega^2=1/c^2$ and $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\varepsilon_0$ $\operatorname{Re}(\overline{e_i}e_j)=\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})$, so all terms combine to $-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$. Clause (d) additionally adopts [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](ii) in the explicitly defined empty-matter model with zero source fields and zero matter energy/momentum densities and fluxes; it applies both balance theorems with zero force and power density and averages their identities: for the $T$-periodic smooth quantities the mean of the time derivative is zero by the fundamental theorem ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), and the remaining flux terms are the averaged quantities just computed, which are constant and hence divergence-free. The average formulas in (a)-(c) are independent of this extra interpretation premise. For the last scope assertion, $e=0$ implies $b=0$ and $u=0$. If $e\ne0$, write $e=a+id$, so $u=\varepsilon_0|a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta|^2$. Choose one coordinate $j$ with $k_j\ne0$ and put $P=2\pi/|k_j|$. At fixed other coordinates and time, integration in $x_j$ over any interval of length $P$ gives $\varepsilon_0P(|a|^2+|d|^2)/2=\varepsilon_0P|e|^2/2$: expand the square and integrate $\cos^2$, $\sin^2$ and $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ over a full period, using the fundamental theorem and $\partial_{x_j}\theta=k_j$. Thus for $R=NP$ with a positive integer $N$, every such section of $[-R,R]^3$ has integral $N\varepsilon_0P|e|^2$. The continuous density and all its sections are Riemann integrable by [[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]. [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] (applied successively, with coordinate reordering justified by the identical finite product-grid Darboux sums) yields $\int_{[-R,R]^3}u=(2R)^2N\varepsilon_0P|e|^2\to\infty$. Nonnegativity and monotonicity of the box integral ([[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]) give divergence along all $R\to\infty$, not only this sequence. No interchange of time and space averages or choice principle is used.
items.physical_scope: Exact period-average identities for an ideal whole-space plane-wave solution of the smooth source-free vacuum Maxwell branch, in a named inertial chart with SI constants: averaged energy density, Poynting flux, momentum density and Maxwell-stress/momentum-flux tensor, with the physical balance reading additionally conditional on Lorentz continuum coupling (ii) in the explicitly defined empty-matter model. Excluded: finite beams and pulses, sources, boundaries, material media, any ensemble or detection statistics, any nonzero finite-total-energy whole-space plane wave, and any empirical claim. The admitted zero amplitude has zero total energy.

items.title: Superposition intensity and the coherent interference cross term
items.statement:
Let $\omega>0$ and let $k_1,k_2\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|k_1|=|k_2|=\omega/c$. For $j=1,2$ let $e_j\in\mathbb C^3$ with
$k_j\cdot e_j=0$, put $b_j=k_j\times e_j/\omega$ and let $(E_j,B_j)$ be the
plane-wave solutions of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] given by
[[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]. Let $a_1,a_2\in\mathbb R$ and put
$(E,B):=a_1(E_1,B_1)+a_2(E_2,B_2)$. Write
$\hat k_j=k_j/|k_j|$, $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|z|^2:=z\cdot\overline z=\sum_{\ell=1}^3|z_\ell|^2$ for $z\in\mathbb C^3$,
and $\langle f\rangle(x):=T^{-1}\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ componentwise.
Then:

(a) [Superposition] $(E,B)$ is a smooth source-free solution of the vacuum
Maxwell equations ([[pthm-em-linear-superposition]]), and at each fixed $x$ it
can be written with a single phase,
$$E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\alpha(x)\,e^{i(k_1\cdot x-\omega t)}),\qquad B(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\beta(x)\,e^{i(k_1\cdot x-\omega t)}),$$
where $\alpha(x):=a_1e_1+a_2e_2e^{i\delta(x)}$,
$\beta(x):=a_1b_1+a_2b_2e^{i\delta(x)}$ and
$\delta(x):=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x$; constant relative phases are absorbed in $e_2$.

(b) [Averaged energy density with the coherent cross term] For every $x$,
$$\langle u\rangle(x)=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|\alpha(x)|^2+\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|\beta(x)|^2=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\bigl(a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2\bigr)+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(W(x)\bigr),$$
where
$W(x):=\bigl(e_1\cdot\overline e_2+(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2)\bigr)e^{-i\delta(x)}$.
The first two terms are the sum of the averaged energy densities of the two
waves ([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]); the third is the interference cross
term, which may remain nonzero after time averaging at fixed relative phase.

(c) [Averaged flux and momentum; equal wavevectors] (with $u$ the energy
density and $S$ the Poynting vector of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]])
$\langle S\rangle(x)=\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\alpha(x)\times\overline{\beta(x)}\bigr)$.
In particular, if $k_1=k_2=:k$ then the superposition is the single plane wave
with amplitude $a_1e_1+a_2e_2$, and
$\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2$,
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2\hat k$
([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]).

(d) [No incoherent or statistical claim] The formulas are deterministic
identities for the specified coherent superposition; they are not an ensemble
average over phases, and no detection statistics, finite-sample visibility
estimate or empirical conclusion is drawn. The computation is a conditional
consequence of the adopted Maxwell postulate and does not by itself distinguish
classical from quantum descriptions of light.
items.strategy: Clause (a): $E_j,B_j$ are source-free smooth solutions of the vacuum Maxwell postulate by [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]](a); the superposition is again such a solution by [[pthm-em-linear-superposition]] (real coefficients). The single-phase rewriting uses $e^{i\theta_2}=e^{i\delta(x)}e^{i\theta_1}$ with $\theta_j=k_j\cdot x-\omega t$ and $\delta=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x$. Clauses (b),(c): at each fixed $x$ write $E=\operatorname{Re}(A e^{-i\omega t})$, $B=\operatorname{Re}(D e^{-i\omega t})$, with $A=\alpha(x)e^{ik_1\cdot x}$ and $D=\beta(x)e^{ik_1\cdot x}$; the common spatial phase cancels in averages and apply the componentwise averages of [[lem-em-period-average]], $\langle\operatorname{Re}(\alpha e^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(\beta e^{-i\omega t})\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\alpha\overline{\beta})$ and the cross-product version; substituting into $u$ and $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] and using $|k_j|=\omega/c$, $b_j=k_j\times e_j/\omega$ together with the identity $(k\times u)\cdot(k\times v)=|k|^2u\cdot v$ for $u,v\perp k$ (from [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]) gives the displayed cross term with $W$: expanding $|\alpha|^2$ gives $a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2+2a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}(e_1\cdot\overline e_2e^{-i\delta})$, and similarly for $\beta$. For $k_1=k_2$ the bracket reduces to $2e_1\cdot\overline e_2$ and the formulas reduce to the single-wave averages of [[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]] for the amplitude $a_1e_1+a_2e_2$. No ensemble or statistical averaging is performed, which is exactly the content of the scope clause (d).
items.physical_scope: Deterministic superposition identities for two same-frequency ideal plane-wave solutions of the smooth source-free vacuum Maxwell branch in a named inertial chart with SI constants: the averaged energy density of the coherent sum with its interference cross term, the averaged Poynting vector, and the equal-wavevector specialization. Excluded: ensembles or random phases, partially coherent and finite sources, detection or sampling statistics, any empirical conclusion, and any claim discriminating classical from quantum descriptions.

items.title: Linear, circular and elliptical amplitude choices
items.statement:
Use the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and the SI conventions of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Fix $K>0$, put
$\omega:=cK$ and $k:=Ke_3$, so that $|k|=K=\omega/c$ and $\hat k=e_3$, and let
$E_0>0$ carry the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$. For each amplitude choice
below put $b:=k\times e/\omega$; then the amplitude conditions of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold and the corresponding fields
$(E,B)$ of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] are smooth source-free vacuum
Maxwell solutions on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, with
$\theta(x,t)=Kx_3-\omega t$.

(i) [Linear] $e:=E_0e_1$, $b=(E_0/c)e_2$. Here $a=E_0e_1$ and $d=0$, the
trace is the segment $[-E_0,E_0]e_1=\{se_1:-E_0\le s\le E_0\}$ traversed
twice per period, the polarization is linear and
$H=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle=0$; moreover
$E=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$, $B=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$ and $|B|=|E|/c$.

(ii) [Circular] $e:=E_0(e_1+ie_2)$, $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-ie_1)$. Here
$a=E_0e_1$ and $d=E_0e_2$, so $|a|=|d|=E_0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=0$: the
polarization is circular of radius $E_0$, with
$E=E_0(\cos\theta\,e_1-\sin\theta\,e_2)$,
$B=(E_0/c)(\sin\theta\,e_1+\cos\theta\,e_2)$, $|E|=E_0$ and $|B|=E_0/c$
everywhere, and $H=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle=E_0^2>0$, so this
polarization is left-handed in the convention of
[[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The reversed choice $e=E_0(e_1-ie_2)$
gives $H=-E_0^2<0$ and is right-handed.

(iii) [Elliptical] $e:=E_0(e_1+2ie_2)$. Here $a=E_0e_1$ and $d=2E_0e_2$ are
orthogonal with unequal lengths, so by clause (b)(iii) of
[[def-em-polarization-definition]] the trace is the axis-aligned ellipse
$E_0\cos\theta\,e_1-2E_0\sin\theta\,e_2$ with semiaxes $E_0$ and $2E_0$ along
$e_1$ and $e_2$; $|E|^2=E_0^2(\cos^2\theta+4\sin^2\theta)$ varies between
$E_0^2$ and $4E_0^2$; and $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-2ie_1)$, $H=2E_0^2>0$.

(iv) [Degenerate and edge cases] $e=0$ gives the zero wave, for which
$a=d=0$ and the trace is the single point $\{0\}$. For $e:=E_0(1+i)e_1$ one
has $a=d=E_0e_1$, so the polarization is linear with trace the segment
$[-\sqrt2E_0,\sqrt2E_0]e_1$ and $H=0$; the classification (b) of
[[def-em-polarization-definition]] covers this case without requiring $a$ and
$d$ to be orthogonal.

(v) [Verification and scope] In every case $b=k\times e/\omega$ with
$|k|=\omega/c$, so the amplitude equations hold and the fields are smooth
source-free solutions by [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]; the amplitudes and
the semiaxis lengths carry the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and
$|B|=|E|/c$ holds pointwise. The examples assert no empirical realization and
no measured polarization.
items.strategy: Direct substitution: for each choice compute $a=\operatorname{Re}e$, $d=\operatorname{Im}e$, the trace $a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$, the helicity sign $H=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle$ with $\hat k=e_3$, and $b=k\times e/\omega$; then apply the classification clauses (b),(c) of [[def-em-polarization-definition]] and the amplitude conditions of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]](b). For (ii) the identity $|E|=E_0$ follows from $|a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta|^2=|a|^2\cos^2\theta+|d|^2\sin^2\theta$ when $\langle a,d\rangle=0$ and $|a|=|d|$. For (iv) the trace values are $E_0(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)$, whose range is $[-\sqrt2E_0,\sqrt2E_0]$. Nothing beyond the listed suppliers is used, and no physical interpretation is added.
items.physical_scope: Explicit ideal plane-wave amplitude choices on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ in a named inertial frame with SI units: linear, circular (both handedness signs), elliptical with orthogonal axes, the zero wave and one dependent-amplitude linear edge case. Excluded: partially polarized light, superposition with other waves, and any empirical or measurement claim.

items.title: A nonzero whole-space plane wave has infinite total energy
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-energy and compact-source comparison branches (ii), (iii), as required by their measure and wave-Cauchy suppliers. The explicit plane-wave fields of (i) use no choice.

Fix $K>0$, $\omega:=cK$, $k:=Ke_3$, $E_0>0$
(unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$), the amplitude $e:=E_0e_1$ and
$b:=k\times e/\omega=(E_0/c)e_2$, and let $(E,B)$ be the corresponding
plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ with energy
density $u$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]; write
$\theta(x,t)=Kx_3-\omega t$. Then:

(i) [Explicit density] $E=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$,
$B=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$ and
$u(x,t)=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2\theta(x,t)$, a nonnegative function vanishing
exactly on the nodal planes $\cos\theta=0$; the period average at every fixed
$x$ is $\langle u\rangle=\varepsilon_0E_0^2/2>0$, uniformly in $x$ and $t$
([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]](a)).

(ii) [Unbounded box integrals] Fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and let
$R\ge(\omega|t|+\pi/4)/K$. On the sub-box
$Q_R:=[-R,R]^2\times[(\omega t-\pi/4)/K,\,(\omega t+\pi/4)/K]$ of the box
$[-R,R]^3$ one has $\cos^2\theta\ge1/2$, hence
$u\ge\varepsilon_0E_0^2/2$ there; both boxes are product boxes with finite
volume ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]), $u$ is continuous on
them and therefore Riemann integrable
([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]), and
monotonicity of the multidimensional Darboux integral
([[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]],
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]) gives
$$\int_{[-R,R]^3}u(x,t)\,dx\;\ge\;\int_{Q_R}u(x,t)\,dx\;\ge\;\frac{\varepsilon_0E_0^2}{2}\,\mathrm{vol}(Q_R)\;=\;\frac{\pi\varepsilon_0E_0^2}{K}\,R^2\;\longrightarrow\;+\infty\quad(R\to\infty).$$
Consequently the box integrals have no finite limit as
$R\to\infty$: the ideal plane wave has infinite total energy in the
box-exhaustion sense, in contrast to the total energy of a single wave 'mode'
being finite on any bounded box.

(iii) [Contrast with compactly supported data] If instead the constrained data
of [[pthm-em-general-wave-ivp]] vanish off a compact set, then by clause (d) of
that theorem the fields have compact spatial support at each time, and the
instantaneous total energy is the integral of the continuous density $u$
over a bounding closed box containing its support, hence finite. So finite total energy is available for
compactly supported data, while the ideal plane wave of (i)-(ii) is not a
finite-energy configuration.

(iv) [Scope] The example is an exact computation for the ideal plane wave; it
reports no measurement, and "infinite total energy" means the divergence
statement (ii), not a claim about any laboratory field or finite beam.
items.strategy: For (i) use $k\times e=(Ke_3)\times(E_0e_1)=KE_0e_2$ and the definitions of $E,B,u$: $u=(\varepsilon_0/2)|E|^2+(1/(2\mu_0))|B|^2=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2\theta$ by $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\varepsilon_0$, and $\langle\cos^2\rangle=1/2$ is the real-amplitude case of [[lem-em-period-average]] (equivalently (a) of [[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]] with $|e|^2=E_0^2$). For (ii) the range condition on $R$ places $Q_R$ inside $[-R,R]^3$; on $Q_R$, $|Kx_3-\omega t|\le\pi/4$ gives $\cos^2\theta\ge1/2$, and the comparison of integrals is the elementary monotonicity of the multidimensional Darboux integral for continuous integrands over boxes, with $\mathrm{vol}(Q_R)=(2R)^2\cdot\pi/(2K)$ from [[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]. The bound is $\pi\varepsilon_0E_0^2R^2/K\to\infty$. Part (iii) quotes clause (d) of [[pthm-em-general-wave-ivp]] and the finite integral of its continuous density over a nondegenerate bounding closed box, with zero density outside. No empirical input is used.
items.physical_scope: An exact computation for one explicit ideal plane-wave configuration on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: the positivity and uniformity of the period-averaged energy density, the divergence of the box integrals, and the contrast with compactly supported finite-energy data. No measured quantity, no finite beam and no empirical claim.

items.title: Ideal absorber and ideal reflector momentum transfer (radiation pressure)
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
[[def-countable-choice]]). Idealised setup: the vacuum region is
$\{x_3<0\}$ and a material body occupies $\{x_3>0\}$ with plane surface
$x_3=0$; an incident plane wave of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] with
$k=Ke_3$ ($K>0$, $\omega=cK$), $e=E_0e_1$ ($E_0>0$, unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$) and $b=(E_0/c)e_2$ propagates in the $+e_3$
direction. By [[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]] its period-averaged Poynting
flux is $\langle S\rangle=I\hat k$ with $I=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}E_0^2$, and
its period-averaged normal Maxwell stress is $\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle=-I/c$
([[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] for $\sigma$). All period-averaged
quantities below are independent of time. Let $A>0$ be the area (in
$\mathrm m^2$) of a finite rectangular surface patch, let
$F\in\mathbb R^3$ be its period-averaged force (in N), and let $p\in\mathbb R$
be the signed normal force per unit area (in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-2}$).
The adopted boundary-force law below sets $F=A p e_3$; these are patch
quantities in the uniform infinite-plane model. Two idealised models of the surface:

(i) [Ideal absorber] Adopt (A1) no reflected vacuum field and a zero back-face
stress for an ideal absorption layer, and (A2) the force on each surface patch
is given by the pillbox limit of the momentum balance, i.e. its signed pressure is the difference
$\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle_{\mathrm{back}}-\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle$ of
the back-face and incident-side normal stresses, with the back-face stress set
to zero by (A1). This is an exterior boundary-force model: the incident vacuum
field is not asserted to extend by zero across a sharp interface as a global
Maxwell solution. A real absorption layer must supply a compatible
material-field solution; no such realization is claimed here. The incident-wave average is constant throughout the vacuum region by
[[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]](c), so its one-sided surface limit is
$\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle=-I/c$. Then the force per unit area is
$p=I/c$ and $F/A=(I/c)\,\hat k$: the wave pushes the absorber along its direction of
propagation with pressure $I/c$.

(ii) [Ideal reflector] Adopt instead (A1') the field on the material side
vanishes identically while the vacuum field is the sum of the incident wave and
the reflected plane wave with $k'=-k$, $e'=-e$ (so that the tangential
electric field vanishes on $x_3=0$; the sum is a source-free solution by
[[pthm-em-linear-superposition]]), together with the same boundary-force law
(A2) with zero material-side stress. Compute the averaged normal stress of the
standing wave directly: the real fields satisfy
$E=E_0[\cos(Kx_3-\omega t)-\cos(Kx_3+\omega t)]e_1=2E_0\sin(Kx_3)\sin(\omega t)e_1$
and $B=(2E_0/c)\cos(Kx_3)\cos(\omega t)e_2$, whose cross terms cancel
identically in $\sigma_{33}=-(\varepsilon_0/2)|E|^2-(1/(2\mu_0))|B|^2$; with
$\langle\sin^2\rangle=\langle\cos^2\rangle=1/2$ this gives
$\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle=-\varepsilon_0E_0^2=-2I/c$ (the incident and
reflected waves contribute $-I/c$ each). Hence $p=2I/c$ and $F/A=(2I/c)\,\hat k$: twice the
absorbing pressure, because the momentum of the reflected wave is reversed.

(iii) [Status] The absorber back-face and reflector vanishing-field
idealisations (A1)/(A1') and the boundary-force law (A2) are adopted model
assumptions of this thought experiment, not derived material laws and not
observations; the deduction from them with the computed averaged stresses is
complete and conditional. The setup idealises an infinite plane beam at normal
incidence on an infinite plane surface; oblique incidence, finite beams, real
absorbers and any magnetisation/current response of a material require a
material model and are excluded. No measured pressure is reported and no
empirical or statistical claim is made.
items.strategy: Deduction from the stated idealisations. Incident wave data: $k\times e=KE_0e_2$, so the amplitudes satisfy [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]](b) and (c) of [[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]] gives $I=\varepsilon_0cE_0^2/2$ and $\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle=-I/c$ for a single monochromatic wave. In (i), the vacuum fields are the incident wave alone, so the already computed constant algebraic average gives $\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle=-I/c$ throughout the vacuum region and its one-sided limit at $0^-$ equals $-I/c$ directly; the force law (A2) then gives $p=I/c$ and $F/A=(I/c)e_3$. In (ii), the standing-wave fields are computed explicitly and averaged with [[lem-em-period-average]]; the cross terms cancel identically in $\sigma_{33}$ because $|E|^2$ and $(c^2)$-weighted $|B|^2$ have opposite cross terms for the two counterpropagating waves, leaving $-\varepsilon_0E_0^2=-2I/c$ at $0^-$, whence $p=2I/c$ and $F/A=(2I/c)e_3$ by (A2). The real-vector trig identities and the substitution $\cos A\pm\cos B$, $\sin A\pm\sin B$ are elementary; the averaged squares use $\langle\cos^2\rangle=\langle\sin^2\rangle=1/2$ from [[lem-em-period-average]]. The direction $\hat k$ is $e_3$, the propagation direction of the incident beam. No material law, absorbed or reflected amplitude, or observed force is derived.
items.physical_scope: Adopted idealisations of a plane beam at normal incidence on an infinite plane ideal absorber or ideal reflector, with the pillbox force law as an explicitly stated model assumption; the conclusion is the conditional pressure $I/c$ or $2I/c$ along the propagation direction. Excluded: oblique incidence, finite beams and pulses, real material response, radiation reaction, measurements, and any empirical claim; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is retained as an assumed premise.

items.title: Ideal deterministic two-wave interference and its fringe geometry
items.statement:
Let $K>0$, $\omega:=cK$, let $\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ (half the angle between the
beams) and $\varphi\in\mathbb R$, and take the two plane waves of
[[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] with
$$k_1=K(\sin\alpha\,e_1+\cos\alpha\,e_3),\qquad k_2=K(-\sin\alpha\,e_1+\cos\alpha\,e_3),$$
$$e_1^{\mathrm{amp}}=E_0e_2,\qquad e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}=E_0e^{i\varphi}e_2,$$
where $E_0>0$ carries $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and both amplitudes are
polarized along $e_2$, perpendicular to both wavevectors; with
$b_j=k_j\times e_j^{\mathrm{amp}}/\omega$ and $|k_j|=\omega/c$ both pairs
satisfy the amplitude equations of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]], so the
superposition is a source-free smooth Maxwell solution
([[pthm-em-classical-interference]]). Write
$\delta(x):=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x=-2K\sin\alpha\,x_1$. Then:

(i) [Averaged energy density]
$\langle u\rangle(x)=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\bigl[1+\cos^2\alpha\,\cos(2K\sin\alpha\,x_1-\varphi)\bigr]$
for every $x$, by clause (b) of [[pthm-em-classical-interference]] with
$e_1^{\mathrm{amp}}\cdot\overline{e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}}=E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}$ and
$(\hat k_1\times e_1^{\mathrm{amp}})\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline{e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}})=E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}\cos2\alpha$.

(ii) [Fringes and visibility] At fixed $x_2,x_3$ the averaged energy density is
periodic in $x_1$ with period $\pi/(K\sin\alpha)=\lambda/(2\sin\alpha)$, where
$\lambda=2\pi/K$; its maximum and minimum are
$\varepsilon_0E_0^2(1\pm\cos^2\alpha)$, so the visibility
$V:=\frac{\langle u\rangle_{\max}-\langle u\rangle_{\min}}{\langle u\rangle_{\max}+\langle u\rangle_{\min}}$
equals $\cos^2\alpha=\frac12(1+\hat k_1\cdot\hat k_2)$. In particular
$V\to1$ as $\alpha\downarrow0$ through crossing beams, and $V\to0$ as
$\alpha\to\pi/2$. At $\alpha=0$ with fixed relative phase the profile is
spatially constant: its spatial visibility is $0$ when its value is positive,
and the displayed ratio is undefined when the field vanishes.

(iii) [The promised copropagating amplitude law] For $k_1=k_2=k$ with $|k|=K$ and $k\cdot e_2=0$, retain the common linear
polarization $e_2$ and amplitudes $E_0e_2$, $E_0e^{i\Delta}e_2$ (so that the
sum is the single plane wave with vector amplitude $E_0(1+e^{i\Delta})e_2$),
$\langle u\rangle=\varepsilon_0E_0^2(1+\cos\Delta)=2\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2(\Delta/2)\propto|1+e^{i\Delta}|^2$,
the form used in the double-slit discussion of the content model. Scanning
$\Delta$ gives phase-scan visibility $1$, distinct from spatial visibility at
fixed phase.

(iv) [Statistical qualifications] This is a deterministic prediction of the
classical wave model for the specified coherent two-wave preparation, at every
point of the ideal plane-wave field; a *measured* fringe pattern or detector
histogram would additionally require a declared measurement model (detector
response, finite bin width, background, integration time, sampling) and a
statistical analysis. The example reports no observation, no finite-sample
claim and no visibility estimate from data; in particular classical
electromagnetic waves interfere, so the prediction alone does not discriminate
between classical and quantum descriptions of light. All quantities are
idealized field quantities of the framework.
items.strategy: Specialise clause (b) of [[pthm-em-classical-interference]] to the stated amplitudes: $|e_j^{\mathrm{amp}}|^2=E_0^2$, $e_1^{\mathrm{amp}}\cdot\overline{e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}}=E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}$, and $\hat k_1\times e_2=\sin\alpha\,e_3-\cos\alpha\,e_1$, $\hat k_2\times e_2=-\sin\alpha\,e_3-\cos\alpha\,e_1$ give $(\hat k_1\times e_2)\cdot(\hat k_2\times e_2)=\cos2\alpha$ by the coordinate cross product [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; the formula (i) follows with $W=2E_0^2\cos^2\alpha\,e^{-i(\delta+\varphi)}$. Part (ii) reads off the period, maxima, minima and visibility from (i). Part (iii) is clause (c) of [[pthm-em-classical-interference]] with $|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2=2E_0^2(1+\cos\Delta)$. Part (iv) is a scope statement: the field-theoretic identities are exact for the specified preparation, and no statistical model or dataset is introduced. No additional supplier is used.
items.physical_scope: A deterministic interference computation for two explicit ideal coherent plane waves of equal frequency and amplitude in a named inertial frame with SI units: averaged energy density, fringe period, visibility and the copropagating amplitude law. Excluded: real sources and detectors, finite coherence and bandwidth, sampling and noise models, finite-sample statistics, and any empirical claim; no discrimination between classical and quantum descriptions is asserted.

items.title: Distinct exponential characters are linearly independent on a nonempty open set, and the real-part grouping rule
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty open set, let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\in\mathbb C^n$ ($m\ge1$) be pairwise distinct, and let $c_1,\dots,c_m\in\mathbb C^q$ for some $q\ge1$ (the scalar case $q=1$ included; all statements below are componentwise). Write $\lambda_j\cdot z$ for the componentwise bilinear extension of the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; the variable $z$ remains real and $e^{iw}$ for the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] at $iw$, and consider the $\mathbb C^q$-valued map $F(z):=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\,e^{i\lambda_j\cdot z}$ on $U$. Then: (a) [Complex independence] if $F(z)=0$ for every $z\in U$, then $c_1=\dots=c_m=0$. (b) [Real-part grouping rule] if $\operatorname{Re}F(z)=0$ for every $z\in U$, then for every $
u\in\mathbb C^n$ the grouped coefficient $$C_
u:=\sum_{\lambda_j=
u} c_j+\sum_{\lambda_j=-\overline
u}\overline{c_j}$$ vanishes; in particular $c_j=0$ whenever $\lambda_j
e-\overline{\lambda_j}$ and $\lambda_j
otin\{\lambda_k,-\overline{\lambda_k}:k
e j\}$. At a self-paired frequency $
u=-\overline
u$ the coefficient is $2\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\lambda_j=
u}c_j$; in particular at $
u=0$ only the real part is constrained, and a purely imaginary coefficient is allowed. (c) [Scope] no hypothesis beyond pairwise distinctness of the $\lambda_j$ and nonemptiness and openness of $U$ is used; $\lambda_j=0$ is allowed and the $\lambda_j$ need not be nonzero, ordered or normalized. The statement concerns the open set $U$ and asserts nothing on sets with empty interior, where distinct characters can agree.
items.strategy:
Proof technique: direct; reduce to the scalar case, conjugate the exponential by its series, prove (a) by induction on the dimension using the one-dimensional annihilating operator $\prod_{j
e j_0}(d/dt-i\lambda_j)$, then obtain (b) by applying (a) to $F+\overline F$ grouped by frequency. 1.1 Reduction to the scalar case. Both assertions are componentwise in $\mathbb C^q$: $F(z)=0$ holds if and only if every component $F_k(z)=\sum_j(c_j)_k e^{i\lambda_j\cdot z}$ vanishes, and $\operatorname{Re}F(z)=0$ if and only if $\operatorname{Re}F_k(z)=0$ for every $k$, while the vector $C_
u$ of clause (b) vanishes if and only if each of its components $\sum_{\lambda_j=
u}(c_j)_k+\sum_{\lambda_j=-\overline
u}\overline{(c_j)_k}$ vanishes. Applying the scalar assertions $q=1$ to each component function therefore yields the general assertions, so we may and do assume $c_1,\dots,c_m\in\mathbb C$ in the rest of the proof. [given, F3, algebra] 1.2 Conjugation of the exponential. For every $w\in\mathbb C$, $\overline{\exp w}=\exp\overline w$. By [F1] the complex numbers $\exp w$ and $\exp\overline w$ are the sums of the everywhere convergent series $\sum_nw^n/n!$ and $\sum_n\overline w^n/n!$, with partial sums $S_N(w)=\sum_{n\le N}w^n/n!$ and $S_N(\overline w)=\sum_{n\le N}\overline w^n/n!$; by [F2] conjugation fixes each real number $n!$ and satisfies $\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w$ and $\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w$, so $\overline{S_N(w)}=S_N(\overline w)$ for every $N$. Also by [F2], $\overline u-\overline v=\overline{u-v}$ and, by the coordinate formula, $|\overline u|=\sqrt{(\operatorname{Re}u)^2+(-\operatorname{Im}u)^2}=|u|$, whence $|\overline u-\overline v|=|u-v|$. Writing $d=\overline{\exp w}-\exp\overline w$, for every $N$ we have $d=(\overline{\exp w}-S_N(\overline w))+(S_N(\overline w)-\exp\overline w)=(\overline{\exp w}-\overline{S_N(w)})+(S_N(\overline w)-\exp\overline w)$, so $|d|\le|\exp w-S_N(w)|+|S_N(\overline w)-\exp\overline w|$; given $\varepsilon>0$, the definition of convergence of the two series supplies $N$ with both summands below $\varepsilon/2$, so $|d|<\varepsilon$, and since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary $|d|=0$, which forces $d=0$ by the definiteness of the modulus in [F2]. [F1, F2, algebra] 1.3 Characters and the annihilating operator. For $\mu\in\mathbb C$ let $\varphi_\mu(t):=\exp(i\mu t)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$, the one-variable restriction of the complex exponential along the real-linear map $t\mapsto i\mu t$. By [F5], the chain rule applied to that map and the entire exponential of [F1] gives $\varphi_\mu'(t)=i\mu\exp(i\mu t)=i\mu\,\varphi_\mu(t)$, and the sum, scalar-multiple and product rules of [F5] give, for any finite combination $\sum_\mu a_\mu\varphi_\mu$ with complex coefficients, derivative $\sum_\mu a_\mu i\mu\,\varphi_\mu$, hence $(d/dt-i\mu)\varphi_\mu=0$ and $(d/dt-i\mu)\varphi_
u=i(
u-\mu)\varphi_
u$ for all $
u\in\mathbb C$. Consequently, for pairwise distinct $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m$ and a fixed $j_0$, the composed operator $L_{j_0}:=\prod_{j
e j_0}(d/dt-i\mu_j)$ is complex-linear on finite combinations and acts on $\varphi_{\mu_k}$ as multiplication by $0$ if $k
e j_0$ and by the constant $\prod_{j
e j_0}i(\mu_{j_0}-\mu_j)$ if $k=j_0$; that constant is nonzero because $i
e0$ and $\mu_{j_0}-\mu_j
e0$ for $j
e j_0$ by pairwise distinctness, and a product of nonzero field elements is nonzero by [F3]. [F1, F3, F5, algebra] 1.4 Induction step: reduction to a product box. Let $n\ge2$ and assume assertion (a) established in dimension $n-1$ for every number of frequencies and every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^{n-1}$. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and open, fix $z^*\in U$ and, by openness, $\varepsilon>0$ with the open product box $B:=\prod_{k=1}^n(z^*_k-\varepsilon,z^*_k+\varepsilon)\subseteq U$; put $B':=\prod_{k=2}^n(z^*_k-\varepsilon,z^*_k+\varepsilon)\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$. Write $z=(z_1,z')$ with $z'\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and $\lambda_j=(\lambda_{j1},\lambda_j')$. For each value $\mu$ in the finite set $\{\lambda_{11},\dots,\lambda_{m1}\}$ put $I_\mu:=\{j:\lambda_{j1}=\mu\}$ and $P_\mu(z'):=\sum_{j\in I_\mu}c_je^{i\lambda_j'\cdot z'}$; then, by the splitting identity of [F4], the exponential addition law of [F1] and the distributivity of the finite sum, $F(z_1,z')=\sum_\mu e^{i\mu z_1}P_\mu(z')$ for every $(z_1,z')\in B$, the outer sum running over the pairwise distinct values $\mu$. [given, F1, F4, algebra] 2.1 Base case, dimension one. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ be nonempty and open, so that it contains a nonempty open interval $J$; suppose $F=\sum_{j=1}^mc_j\varphi_{\lambda_j}\equiv0$ on $U$. Fix $j_0$; then $L_{j_0}F\equiv0$ on $J$, and by step 1.3 and the linearity of $L_{j_0}$ we have $L_{j_0}F=c_{j_0} igl(\prod_{j
e j_0}i(\lambda_{j_0}-\lambda_j) igr)\varphi_{\lambda_{j_0}}$ on $J$. Choose $t_0\in J$. Evaluating there gives $c_{j_0} igl(\prod_{j
e j_0}i(\lambda_{j_0}-\lambda_j) igr)\exp(i\lambda_{j_0}t_0)=0$; cancelling the nonzero exponential by [F1] gives $c_{j_0}\prod_{j
e j_0}i(\lambda_{j_0}-\lambda_j)=0$; the second factor is a product of nonzero complex numbers, hence nonzero by [F3], so $c_{j_0}=0$ by the field property in [F3]. As $j_0$ was arbitrary, $c_1=\dots=c_m=0$; this proves (a) for $n=1$. [given, step 1.3, F1, F3] 2.2 The conjugate sum. Suppose now that $\operatorname{Re}F\equiv0$ on $U$, and define $\widetilde F(z):=\sum_{j=1}^m\overline{c_j}\,e^{-i\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z}$ on $U$. For real $z$ and every $j$, step 1.2 applied to $w=i\lambda_j\cdot z$ gives $\overline{e^{i\lambda_j\cdot z}}=\exp igl(\overline{i\lambda_j\cdot z} igr)$, and by [F2] and the reality of $z$ we have $\overline{i\lambda_j\cdot z}=\overline i\,\overline{\lambda_j\cdot z}=(-i) igl(\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z igr)=-i\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z$; therefore $\overline{F(z)}=\sum_j\overline{c_j}\,e^{-i\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z}=\widetilde F(z)$ on $U$ by [F2]. Since $w+\overline w=2\operatorname{Re}w$ by [F2], the hypothesis $2\operatorname{Re}F\equiv0$ reads $F+\widetilde F\equiv0$ on $U$. [given, step 1.2, F2] 3.1 One-dimensional slices. Suppose $F\equiv0$ on $U$, fix $z'\in B'$ and define $G(t):=\sum_\mu e^{i\mu t}P_\mu(z')$ for $t$ in the interval $J:=(z^*_1-\varepsilon,z^*_1+\varepsilon)$. By step 1.4, $G(t)=F(t,z')=0$ for every $t\in J$, and $G$ is a finite combination of the pairwise distinct characters $\varphi_\mu$ with complex coefficients $P_\mu(z')$; the base case of step 2.1 applied on the nonempty open interval $J$ therefore gives $P_\mu(z')=0$ for every $\mu$. As $z'\in B'$ was arbitrary, each $P_\mu$ vanishes identically on the nonempty open set $B'$. [step 2.1, step 1.4] 4.1 Induction hypothesis on each group. Fix a value $\mu$. The vectors $\lambda_j'$, $j\in I_\mu$, are pairwise distinct: if $\lambda_j'=\lambda_k'$ and $\lambda_{j1}=\lambda_{k1}=\mu$, then $\lambda_j=\lambda_k$, hence $j=k$ by pairwise distinctness of the $\lambda_j$. The function $P_\mu=\sum_{j\in I_\mu}c_je^{i\lambda_j'\cdot z'}$ vanishes identically on the nonempty open set $B'\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, so assertion (a) in dimension $n-1$ gives $c_j=0$ for every $j\in I_\mu$. Every index lies in $I_{\lambda_{j1}}$, so $c_1=\dots=c_m=0$; this completes the induction and proves (a) in every dimension $n\ge1$. [step 3.1, step 1.4, induction] 5.1 Frequency grouping and application of part (a). Let $\Phi\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be the finite set of distinct values among $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m,-\overline{\lambda_1},\dots,-\overline{\lambda_m}$, and for $
u\in\Phi$ put $C_
u:=\sum_{j:\lambda_j=
u}c_j+\sum_{j:-\overline{\lambda_j}=
u}\overline{c_j}=\sum_{\lambda_j=
u}c_j+\sum_{\lambda_j=-\overline
u}\overline{c_j}$. Regrouping the finite sum of step 2.2 over the distinct frequencies and using the bilinearity of the extended inner product in [F4] gives $F+\widetilde F=\sum_{
u\in\Phi}C_
u e^{i
u\cdot z}$ on $U$; the frequencies $
u\in\Phi$ are pairwise distinct by construction, so assertion (a) as proved in steps 2.1 and 4.1 applied to this finite combination gives $C_
u=0$ for every $
u\in\Phi$. For $
u
otin\Phi$ both defining sums are empty, so $C_
u=0$ trivially; hence $C_
u=0$ for every $
u\in\mathbb C^n$. [given, step 2.2, step 4.1, F4, algebra] 6.1 Consequences and scope. (i) If $
u=-\overline
u$ is self-paired, the condition $-\overline{\lambda_j}=
u$ is equivalent to $\lambda_j=
u$, so both sums of $C_
u$ run over the same index set and $C_
u=\sum_{\lambda_j=
u}(c_j+\overline{c_j})=2\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\lambda_j=
u}c_j$ by [F2]; at $
u=0$ this constrains only the real part, and the constraint is genuinely not stronger: for $m=1$, $\lambda_1=0$, $q=1$ and $c_1=i$ one has $F\equiv i$, so $\operatorname{Re}F\equiv0$ and $C_0=c_1+\overline{c_1}=2\operatorname{Re}i=0$, a nonzero purely imaginary coefficient at frequency $0$. (ii) If $\lambda_j
e-\overline{\lambda_j}$ and $\lambda_j
otin\{\lambda_k,-\overline{\lambda_k}:k
e j\}$, then $\{k:\lambda_k=\lambda_j\}=\{j\}$ and $\{k:\lambda_k=-\overline{\lambda_j}\}=\emptyset$ (a member $k=j$ would give $\lambda_j=-\overline{\lambda_j}$, and $k
e j$ is excluded by hypothesis), so $C_{\lambda_j}=c_j+0=c_j=0$ by step 5.1, which is the stated consequence. (iii) The scope (c) holds: steps 2.1, 1.4 and 4.1 used only pairwise distinctness of the $\lambda_j$ and the nonemptiness and openness of $U$, through the interval $J$ and the product box $B$; the frequencies were never assumed nonzero, ordered or normalized; the proof is a finite construction using complex arithmetic, the series for the exponential and its derivative, and no choice principle. No assertion is made for sets of empty interior: the openness of $U$ is used when a nonempty open interval and a product box are extracted from it, and the statement (c) records that distinct characters can agree on such smaller sets. [step 5.1, step 2.2, F1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

items.title: The two-equation interface admittance system: solution formulas and the normal-flux identity
items.statement:
Let $Y_1,Y_2\in\mathbb C$ with $Y_1+Y_2
e0$, and let $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$ satisfy the two linear equations $$E_i+E_r=E_t,\qquad Y_1(E_i-E_r)=Y_2E_t.$$ Then: (a) [Solution] If $E_i
e0$, then $$r:= rac{E_r}{E_i}= rac{Y_1-Y_2}{Y_1+Y_2},\qquad t:= rac{E_t}{E_i}= rac{2Y_1}{Y_1+Y_2};$$ if $E_i=0$ then $E_r=E_t=0$ and the field ratios are undefined. Throughout (b)-(d), $r,t$ denote the displayed algebraic transfer coefficients $(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$, which are defined independently of $E_i$; when $E_i
e0$ they equal the field ratios of (a). (b) [Normal-flux identity] If $Y_1>0$ is real (the incident side admittance), then $$|r|^2+ rac{\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{Y_1}\,|t|^2=1,$$ and explicitly $|t|^2=\dfrac{4Y_1^2}{|Y_1+Y_2|^2}$ and $|r|^2=1-\dfrac{4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{|Y_1+Y_2|^2}$. The second summand $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2$ is nonnegative if and only if $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\ge0$; it is the normal-flux coefficient of a passive transmitted medium and may be negative for an active one, in which case $|r|>1$ and the identity carries no energy-conservation reading. (c) [Pure-imaginary admittance] If $Y_1>0$ is real and $Y_2$ is purely imaginary, then $|r|=1$, $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\,|t|^2=0$ and $|t|^2=\dfrac{4Y_1^2}{Y_1^2+|Y_2|^2}>0$; in particular $r
e0$ and $t
e0$. (d) [Real-positive specialisation] If $Y_1,Y_2>0$ are real, then $r=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$ are real and $|r|^2+(Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$; with $Y_j=1/Z_j$, $Z_j>0$, this is $r=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_1+Z_2)$, $t=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$ and $R+T=1$ for $R=|r|^2$, $T=(Z_1/Z_2)|t|^2$, in agreement with [[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]]. (e) [Scope] The lemma is pure algebra of $\mathbb C$; the labels 'incident', 'reflected' and 'transmitted' and the interpretation of the second summand as a flux fraction belong to the consuming physical theorem, not to this lemma.
items.strategy:
Proof technique: direct; solve the two linear equations by substitution, expand the moduli with $|z|^2=z\overline z$, and read the sign statements off the ordered-field structure of $\mathbb R$. 1.1 [Solution of the linear system] Substituting the first equation $E_r=E_t-E_i$ into the second gives $Y_1(2E_i-E_t)=Y_2E_t$, that is $2Y_1E_i=(Y_1+Y_2)E_t$ after expanding and collecting terms by the field arithmetic of [F1]. Since $Y_1+Y_2
e0$ is invertible in the field $\mathbb C$ by [F1], $E_t=2Y_1E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)$, and then $E_r=E_t-E_i= igl(2Y_1-(Y_1+Y_2) igr)E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)=(Y_1-Y_2)E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)$, again by [F1]. [given, F1, algebra] 2.1 [Consequences of the solution] If $E_i
e0$, dividing the two identities of step 1.1 by $E_i$ gives $r=E_r/E_i=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=E_t/E_i=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$. If $E_i=0$, the identities of step 1.1 give $E_t=0$ and $E_r=0$, so no field ratio exists; the algebraic expressions $r=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$ remain defined because $Y_1+Y_2
e0$, and they agree with the field ratios whenever the latter exist. This proves (a) and the convention stated before (b). [step 1.1, F1, algebra] 3.1 [Modular expansions] For any $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $|z\pm w|^2=(z\pm w)(\overline z\pm\overline w)=|z|^2\pm(z\overline w+\overline z w)+|w|^2$, and $z\overline w+\overline z w=2\operatorname{Re}(z\overline w)$ by [F2]; hence for real $Y_1$ and arbitrary $Y_2$, $|Y_1\pm Y_2|^2=Y_1^2\pm2Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2+|Y_2|^2$, and subtraction gives $|Y_1+Y_2|^2-|Y_1-Y_2|^2=4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2$. Moreover $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$ and $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$: indeed $|zw|=|z||w|$ and $|z|^2=z\overline z$ by [F2] applied to the quotients of step 2.1 give $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}$ and $|t|^2=|2Y_1|^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}=4Y_1^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}$ because $(2Y_1)\overline{(2Y_1)}=4Y_1^2$ for real $Y_1$, and the denominator is nonzero since $Y_1+Y_2
e0$. [step 2.1, F2, algebra] 4.1 [The flux identity] Assume $Y_1>0$ real. By [F2] and [F3], $|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$, so $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$, and the identity of step 3.1 gives $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2=1-4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$; adding $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$ cancels the correction and yields $|r|^2+(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$, the displayed identity and explicit formulas of (b). [step 3.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra] 5.1 [Sign analysis] Still with $Y_1>0$ real: since $|t|^2>0$ by step 4.1, the second summand $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2$ has the sign of $\operatorname{Re}Y_2$ by [F3], so it is nonnegative if and only if $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\ge0$. If $\operatorname{Re}Y_2<0$, then $|r|^2=1-4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>1$, and since $|r|\ge0$ and $1\ge0$, [F4] gives $|r|>1$; in that case the identity of step 4.1 has a negative transmitted term and carries no energy-conservation reading, while $|r|>1$ alone is consistent with an active transmitted model. [step 4.1, F3, F4, algebra] 5.2 [Purely imaginary admittance] Assume $Y_1>0$ real and $Y_2=i eta$ with $ eta\in\mathbb R$. Then $\overline{Y_1+Y_2}=Y_1-i eta=Y_1-Y_2$ by [F2], so $|Y_1-Y_2|=|\overline{Y_1+Y_2}|=|Y_1+Y_2|$ by [F2] and step 3.1 gives $|r|=1$; the identity of step 4.1 then gives $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\,|t|^2=0$ (multiplying the identity by $Y_1>0$ and using $|r|^2=1$), while $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2=4Y_1^2/(Y_1^2+ eta^2)=4Y_1^2/(Y_1^2+|Y_2|^2)>0$ by [F2] and [F3]; hence $r
e0$ because $|r|=1$ and $t
e0$ because $|t|>0$ by the definiteness of the modulus in [F2]. This proves (c); no division by $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=0$ is performed, and the case $Y_2=0$ is included with $ eta=0$. [step 4.1, step 3.1, F2, F3, algebra] 5.3 [Real-positive specialisation] Assume $Y_1,Y_2>0$ real. Then $Y_1-Y_2$ is real and $Y_1+Y_2>0$ is real and nonzero, so $r,t$ of step 2.1 are real by [F1], and step 4.1 gives $|r|^2+(Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$ because $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=Y_2$. Substituting $Y_j=1/Z_j$ with $Z_j>0$ real, $Y_j$ is invertible and $1/Z_1\pm1/Z_2=(Z_2\pm Z_1)/(Z_1Z_2)$ by [F1], so $r=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_1+Z_2)$ and $t=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$ by cancellation of the nonzero factor $Z_1Z_2$; moreover $Y_2/Y_1=Z_1/Z_2$ by [F1], so the balance is $R+T=1$ for $R=|r|^2$ and $T=(Z_1/Z_2)|t|^2$. These are exactly the solution formulas and the balance of [F5], so clause (d) is in agreement with [[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]]. [step 4.1, step 2.1, F1, F5, algebra] 6.1 [Scope] Clause (e) holds: the entire argument is algebra in the field $\mathbb C$ together with the ordered-field arithmetic of the real scalars $Y_1,\operatorname{Re}Y_2$; no wave model, no labelling of the amplitudes and no interpretation of the second summand is used, and no choice principle occurs, all divisions being by explicitly nonzero field elements. [given, F1, F5, algebra] ∎

items.title: Homogeneous isotropic medium parameters: phase speed, impedance, refractive index, complex propagation constant and skin depth
items.statement: Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], in its isotropic scalar case: the material is at rest in the laboratory frame, and the constitutive relations of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]] hold with constant scalars $\varepsilon>0$ (F$\,$m$^{-1}$), $\mu>0$ (H$\,$m$^{-1}$) and $\sigma\ge0$ (S$\,$m$^{-1}$), so that $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ and the free current is $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Write $c>0$ for the exact vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and let $\omega>0$ (s$^{-1}$) be an angular frequency. Define: (a) [Lossless parameters] with $\sqrt{\cdot}$ the nonnegative square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]], $$v:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}\quad(\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}),\qquad Z:=\Bigl(\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^{1/2}\quad(\Omega),\qquad n:=\frac{c}{v}=c(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}\quad(\text{dimensionless}),\qquad k(\omega):=\frac{\omega}{v};$$ $v$ is the phase speed, $Z$ the wave impedance, $n$ the refractive index relative to vacuum and $k(\omega)$ the real wavenumber of the lossless case. (b) [Complex propagation constant] put $a:=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}>0$, $b:=\mu\sigma\omega\ge0$, $r:=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ and $$p(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r+a}{2}},\qquad q(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r-a}{2}},\qquad \kappa(\omega):=p(\omega)+i\,q(\omega).$$ Then $\kappa(\omega)$ is the unique $k\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}k\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}k\ge0$ and $k^{2}=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega=a+ib$; in the lossless case $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $q=0$ and $\kappa(\omega)=k(\omega)=p(\omega)$ real. (The explicit formula is the one of [[thm-every-complex-number-has-a-square-root]]; the verification $p^{2}-q^{2}=a$, $2pq=b$ and the uniqueness of the root with $\operatorname{Re}k\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}k\ge0$ are verified in the well-definedness paragraph below.) (c) [Skin depth] call $\delta(\omega):=1/q(\omega)$ (m) the skin depth if $\sigma>0$, and set $\delta(\omega):=+\infty$ if $\sigma=0$: for $\kappa(\omega)=p+iq$ and $x_3\in\mathbb R$ the modulus of $e^{i(\kappa x_3-\omega t)}$ equals $e^{-q x_3}$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]), so $\delta$ is the distance in which that modulus decays by the factor $1/e$ in the direction of increasing $x_3$; for $\sigma=0$ there is no attenuation and $\delta$ is infinite rather than a division by zero. (d) [Status and scope] This item fixes objects, units, branch conventions and terminology only. It asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation for a solution, no attenuation of any concrete field and no material validity. The parameters are declared for the isotropic scalar constant-coefficient branch at rest in the laboratory frame; for $\varepsilon\mu<c^{-2}$ the branch is, by [[post-em-material-closure]](b), a declared finite-band effective phase-response model with no universal front-speed claim, while $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$ is the exact broadband case. No measured value, precision or empirical statement is included.
items.strategy: The material assumptions, the rest-frame clause, the isotropic scalar case and the finite-band caveat are those of [[post-em-material-closure]](a)-(b) read with [[def-em-polarization-magnetization|the polarization and magnetization definitions]]; the unit system and the exact constant $c$ are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; the laboratory chart is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. The only content beyond notation is the well-definedness of $\kappa(\omega)$ in (b). With $a>0$, $b\ge0$ and $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ one has $r+a>0$ and $(r-a)(r+a)=b^2\ge0$, so $r-a\ge0$ and both defining radicands are nonnegative. If $b>0$, the same identity gives $r-a>0$, hence $q>0$; if $b=0$, uniqueness of nonnegative roots gives $r=a$ and $q=0$. Also $p>0$ because $r+a>0$. Thus $p^{2}-q^{2}=(r+a)/2-(r-a)/2=a$ and $(2pq)^{2}=4\cdot(r+a)(r-a)/4=r^{2}-a^{2}=b^{2}$, so $2pq=b$ because $p,q\ge0$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); hence $\kappa^{2}=p^{2}-q^{2}+2ipq=a+ib$, by the field arithmetic of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. The square roots of $a+ib$ are exactly $\pm\kappa$: if $z^2=\kappa^2$, then $(z-\kappa)(z+\kappa)=0$, and the complex field property ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) gives $z=\kappa$ or $z=-\kappa$. If $k=u+iv$ with $u,v\ge0$ and $k^{2}=a+ib$, then $u^{2}-v^{2}=a$, $2uv=b$ and $u^{2}+v^{2}=|k|^{2}=|k^{2}|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}=r$, where $|k^{2}|=|k|^{2}$ is the multiplicativity of the modulus ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) and $|a+ib|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ is the modulus of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]; solving gives $u^{2}=(r+a)/2=p^{2}$ and $v^{2}=(r-a)/2=q^{2}$, and since $u,v,p,q\ge0$ the uniqueness of the nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]) gives $u=p$ and $v=q$, so $k=\kappa$. In the lossless case $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $r=a$, $q=0$, $p=\sqrt a=\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}=k(\omega)$ by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. All divisions are by strictly positive real numbers, $v$ and $q$ are nonzero exactly where defined, and no choice principle is used.
items.physical_scope: Terminology, units and branch conventions for homogeneous isotropic materials at rest in the laboratory frame in the constant scalar branch D=eps E, B=mu H, J_f=sigma E+J_ext with eps,mu>0 and sigma>=0: the lossless phase speed, wave impedance, refractive index and wavenumber, the complex propagation constant kappa=p+iq as the unique root with Re,Im>=0 of k^2=eps*mu*omega^2+i*mu*sigma*omega, and the skin depth. Objects, units and conventions only: no field equation, no dispersion relation for a solution, no attenuation of any concrete field and no material validity or measured value.

items.title: Plane-wave fields in a homogeneous Ohmic medium: amplitude conditions, dispersion, averaged flux and the evanescent branch
items.reference: core-conditional-proofs.md#K8 (admittance and flux ingredients); scaffold-added necessary prerequisite (see research/physics-em-sr-40-2026-10-08-batch-34.notes.md)
items.statement:
Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in its isotropic scalar case at rest in the laboratory frame, with constants $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ and $\sigma\ge0$, the constitutive relations $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], the macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], the fields of [[def-em-fields]] on the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and the parameters and phase convention of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]. Consider a declared region with vanishing free charge density and no external free current, so that $ho_f=0$ and the free current is the conduction current $J_f=\sigma E$. Let $k\in\mathbb C^{3}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,h\in\mathbb C^{3}$, and for $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^{3}	imes\mathbb R$ define $E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re} igl(e\,e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)} igr)$ and $H(x,t):=\operatorname{Re} igl(h\,e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)} igr)$ componentwise, i.e. with the phase convention $e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}$ and the real-part encoding of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; put $D:=\varepsilon E$, $B:=\mu H$ and $J_f:=\sigma E$. Extend the Euclidean inner and cross products to $\mathbb C^{3}$ by the same componentwise polynomial formulas ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]). For a complex vector $z\in\mathbb C^3$, use the Hermitian norm $|z|:=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^3|z_j|^2}$, so $|z|^2=z\cdot\overline z=|\operatorname{Re}z|^2+|\operatorname{Im}z|^2$; the dot product itself remains complex bilinear. Then: (a) [Amplitude vanishing] if $\operatorname{Re} igl(w\,e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)} igr)=0$ for some $w\in\mathbb C^{3}$ and all $(x,t)$ in a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^{3}	imes\mathbb R$, then $w=0$. (b) [Amplitude conditions] the quadruple $(E,H,D,B)$ satisfies the four source-free macroscopic equations $\operatorname{div}D=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ on $\mathbb R^{3}	imes\mathbb R$ if and only if $$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot h=0,\qquad k	imes e=\omega\mu\,h,\qquad k	imes h=-(\omega\varepsilon+i\sigma)\,e .$$ (c) [Structure, dispersion and solution family] if $e
e0$ and (b) holds, then $h=k	imes e/(\omega\mu)$, $k\cdot h=0$, $e\cdot h=0$ and $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega$; conversely, if $k\in\mathbb C^{3}\setminus\{0\}$ and $\omega>0$ satisfy $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega$, then for every $e\in\mathbb C^{3}$ with $k\cdot e=0$ the pair $(e,\,k	imes e/(\omega\mu))$ satisfies (b), with $(e,h)=(0,0)$ if and only if $e=0$; on the dispersion relation the solution set of (b) for fixed $(k,\omega)$ is exactly $\{(e,\,k	imes e/(\omega\mu)):k\cdot e=0\}$, a complex two-dimensional space when $k
e0$; off the dispersion relation the only solution is $e=h=0$. (d) [Lossless propagating waves: instantaneous identities and period averages] if (b) holds and $\sigma=0$ and $k\in\mathbb R^{3}$ with $e
e0$, then $|k|^{2}=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}$, $|k|=k(\omega)$ in the notation of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]], and for every $(x,t)$ $k\cdot E=k\cdot B=0$, $E\cdot B=0$, $B=\hat k	imes E/v$ and $|B|=|E|/v$ with $\hat k=k/|k|$; the period-$T$ averages with $T=2\pi/\omega$ ([[lem-em-period-average]]) satisfy, for $u=	frac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$ and $S=E	imes H$ of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]], $$\langle uangle= rac{\varepsilon}{2}|e|^{2},\qquad \langle Sangle= rac{|e|^{2}}{2\mu\omega}\,k= rac{|e|^{2}}{2Z}\,\hat k=v\,\langle uangle\hat k .$$ (e) [Evanescent waves] if $\sigma=0$, $n'\in\mathbb R^{3}$ is a unit vector, $k=\kappa_0+i eta n'$ with $\kappa_0\in\mathbb R^{3}$, $\kappa_0\cdot n'=0$, $ eta>0$ and $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}$ (so $|\kappa_0|^{2}=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+ eta^{2}$ and $\kappa_0
e0$; define $\hat\kappa_0:=\kappa_0/|\kappa_0|$), and if $e
e0$ satisfies $k\cdot e=0$ with $h:=k	imes e/(\omega\mu)$, then the field factorizes exactly as $E(x,t)=e^{- eta\,n'\cdot x}\,\operatorname{Re} igl(e\,e^{i(\kappa_0\cdot x-\omega t)} igr)$, and the time-averaged flux satisfies $\langle Sangle=e^{-2 eta n'\cdot x}\,	frac12\operatorname{Re}(e	imes\overline h)$ with normal component $\langle S\cdot n'angle=-\dfrac{e^{-2 eta n'\cdot x}}{2\mu\omega}\operatorname{Re} igl[(e\cdot n')(\kappa_0\cdot\overline e) igr]$; this normal component is in fact zero for every such transverse amplitude. For the transverse-electric polarisation $e=E_0(n'	imes\hat\kappa_0)$, $E_0\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, and for the transverse-magnetic data $h=H_0\hat y'$ with $\hat y':=n'	imes\hat\kappa_0$, $H_0\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ and electric amplitude $e=-(k	imes\hat y')H_0/(\omega\varepsilon)$, the normal component vanishes identically, $\langle S\cdot n'angle\equiv0$, while the tangential averaged flux is positive: $\langle S\cdot\hat\kappa_0angle=\dfrac{|\kappa_0||e|^{2}}{2\mu\omega}e^{-2 eta n'\cdot x}>0$ in the transverse-electric case and $\langle S\cdot\hat\kappa_0angle=\dfrac{|\kappa_0||h|^{2}}{2\omega\varepsilon}e^{-2 eta n'\cdot x}>0$ in the transverse-magnetic case. (f) [Scope] the four equations are verified only for the explicit ideal whole-space plane-wave fields; for $k$ with $\operatorname{Im}k
e0$ the factor $e^{-\operatorname{Im}k\cdot x}$ grows in some directions, so clauses (b)-(e) are read on regions where the model declares the field bounded (in (e), on the half-space $n'\cdot x>0$). No completeness, energy-finiteness, boundary, interface, material-validity or empirical claim is made, and the finite-band caveat of [[post-em-material-closure]](b) applies whenever $\varepsilon\mu<c^{-2}$.

Proof technique: direct; exhibit the partial derivatives of the encoded fields, reduce each equation to a complex coefficient identity by the amplitude-vanishing fact, analyse the resulting algebraic system, and compute the lossless and evanescent structures with the period-average supplier. 1.1 [Derivatives of the encoded fields] For $w\in\mathbb C^3$ and $	heta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$, each component $x\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w_j\exp(i	heta(x,t)))$ has partial derivatives $\partial_{x_l}\operatorname{Re}(w_j\exp(i	heta))=\operatorname{Re} igl(i\,k_l\,w_j\exp(i	heta) igr)$ and $\partial_t\operatorname{Re}(w_j\exp(i	heta))=\operatorname{Re} igl(-i\omega\,w_j\exp(i	heta) igr)$: indeed $	heta$ is the real-linear map $(x,t)\mapsto\sum_lk_lx_l-\omega t$ with partial derivatives $k_l$ in $x_l$ and $-\omega$ in $t$ as derivatives of line maps by [F4], and the chain rule [F2] applied to the entire exponential gives $\partial_{x_l}\exp(i	heta)=ik_l\exp(i	heta)$ and $\partial_t\exp(i	heta)=-i\omega\exp(i	heta)$, after which the real-linear coordinate projection $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with taking the derivative by [F1]. The complex multipliers stay inside $\operatorname{Re}$. Consequently $\operatorname{div}D=\varepsilon\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\cdot e\,e^{i	heta})$, $\operatorname{div}B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\cdot h\,e^{i	heta})$, $\operatorname{curl}E=\operatorname{Re}(i\,k	imes e\,e^{i	heta})$, $\partial_tB=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\mu\,h\,e^{i	heta})$, $\operatorname{curl}H=\operatorname{Re}(i\,k	imes h\,e^{i	heta})$ and $J_f+\partial_tD=\operatorname{Re} igl((\sigma-i\omega\varepsilon)e\,e^{i	heta} igr)$ with the componentwise complex inner and cross products of [F5] and the uniform notation $e^{i	heta}:=\exp(i	heta)$. e0$: by [F2], $\exp w\exp(-w)=\exp 0=1$, and a product equal to $1

Fix $(x_0,t_0)\in Z$; by openness of $Z$ there is $\delta>0$ with $\{x_0\}	imes(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)\subseteq Z$. The components of the map $t\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(W\exp(-i\omega t))$ with $W:=w\,e^{ik\cdot x_0}$ vanish on that interval, and by step 1.1 its $t$-derivative is $\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega W\exp(-i\omega t))$, so at $t_0$ both $\operatorname{Re}(W\exp(-i\omega t_0))=0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega W\exp(-i\omega t_0))=0$. Writing $W\exp(-i\omega t_0)=u+iv$ with real coordinate vectors $u,v$ by [F3], the first identity is $u=0$ and the second is $\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega(u+iv))=\omega v=0$; since $\omega>0$, $v=0$; hence $W\exp(-i\omega t_0)=0$, and since $\exp(-i\omega t_0)
e0$ by step 1.2 the field property in [F3] gives $W=0$, i.e. $w\,e^{ik\cdot x_0}=0$, and $\exp(ik\cdot x_0)
e0$ by step 1.2 gives $w=0$. This proves (a). [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, F2, F3] 3.1 [Equations as coefficient identities] By step 1.1 the four equations of (b) are, on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$, the identities $\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\cdot e\,e^{i	heta})=0$, $\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\cdot h\,e^{i	heta})=0$, $\operatorname{Re}(i\,k	imes e\,e^{i	heta})+\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\mu\,h\,e^{i	heta})=0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(i\,k	imes h\,e^{i	heta})-\operatorname{Re} igl((\sigma-i\omega\varepsilon)e\,e^{i	heta} igr)=0$; all fields are smooth on the open set $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$, so the operators of [F4] apply. By the additivity of $\operatorname{Re}$ in [F1] and [F3], each of these is an identity $\operatorname{Re}(W_j\,e^{i	heta})=0$ for a constant scalar or vector $W_j$ (embedding a scalar as $(W_j,0,0)$ to apply (a)); by (a) of step 2.1, with the open set $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$, they hold if and only if the constants vanish. The third holds if and only if $i\,k	imes e-i\omega\mu\,h=0$, that is $k	imes e=\omega\mu\,h$ after dividing by the nonzero factor $i$ and using $\omega\mu

With the positively oriented orthonormal triad $(\hat\kappa_0,\hat y',n')$ where $\hat y'=n'	imes\hat\kappa_0$, the cross-product relations $\hat y'	imes n'=\hat\kappa_0$ and $\hat y'	imes\hat\kappa_0=-n'$ hold by [F5], so $e	imes\overline h=|E_0|^2 igl[|\kappa_0|\hat\kappa_0-i eta n' igr]/(\omega\mu)$ and $\langle S\cdot\hat\kappa_0angle=e^{-2 eta n'\cdot x}|E_0|^2|\kappa_0|/(2\mu\omega)=e^{-2 eta n'\cdot x}|e|^2|\kappa_0|/(2\mu\omega)>0$ because $|e|^2=|E_0|^2
e0$, $|\kappa_0|>0$ and $\mu,\omega,v>0$. In the transverse-magnetic case $h=H_0\hat y'$ with $H_0

[step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, step 4.1, F3, F5, F7, algebra] 11.1 [Scope (f)] Clause (f) holds: all computations were carried out for the explicit fields defined by $(k,\omega,e,h)$ on the whole space, so no existence or completeness of any plane-wave family, no energy finiteness, no boundary or interface conditions, no material validity and no empirical statement is claimed; for $\operatorname{Im}k

items.physical_scope: Exact conditional statement about ideal plane-wave fields in a homogeneous isotropic Ohmic medium at rest, on the laboratory chart: the four macroscopic equations hold if and only if the four complex amplitude conditions hold, with the dispersion relation, transverse structure, lossless period-averaged energy density and flux, and the evanescent decay and normal-flux identities. Excluded: general bounded-field or finite-energy existence theory, interfaces, anisotropic or dispersive media, nonlinear response, ideal conductors, any completeness of the plane-wave family, and all empirical statements.
